title: Fair tests, step two: repeat, average and say only what you found

summary.text: A paper spinner dropped from the same hand, five times, takes five slightly different times to land. Nothing was changed, and yet nothing repeated exactly. So when a longer wing seems to make the spinner fall slower, how can anyone tell the wing from the wobble? Your child names the three jobs in a test, tries more than two amounts, repeats each measurement, and works out an average and a range. They test paper spinners and paper bridges, learn what to do with an odd result, and write conclusions that say no more than the results show. They also meet Tu Youyou, who found a medicine by changing one hidden thing in how a plant was prepared.
summary.art: Three paper spinners of different wing lengths falling past a ruler on a wall, with a hand holding a phone stopwatch.

intro.hook: Drop a paper spinner and time how long it takes to land. Now drop it again in exactly the same way. The time is different. Do it a third time. Different again. You changed nothing, and the numbers still do not match.
intro.text: So here is the puzzle. If the same spinner gives different times, how can you tell that a longer wing made it fall slower? Maybe the wing did it, or maybe it was just the wobble. In this unit you learn how scientists deal with the wobble. They name what they change, what they measure and what they keep the same. They repeat each measurement, and they look at the average and at how far the numbers spread. Then they write a conclusion that does not say more than the numbers do.
intro.art: A paper spinner at three moments in its fall beside a stopwatch showing three slightly different times.

outcomes: I can name the three jobs in a test: the thing I change, the thing I measure, and the things I keep the same.
I can try more than two amounts of the thing I change, so I can see a pattern.
I can explain why measuring the same thing again gives slightly different numbers, and repeat a measurement several times.
I can work out an average and a range, and say what each one tells me.
I can spot an odd result, check it, and decide what to do with it without hiding it.
I can show results in a table, a bar chart or a line graph, and say which suits the question.
I can write a conclusion with a claim, evidence and reasoning that says no more than the results show.
I can tell a pattern from a cause, and say how hoping for a result can bend a test.

terms.meaning: Anything in a test that can change, such as the length of a wing, the height of a drop or the time of day.
terms.example: In a spinner test, the wing length, the paper, the clip and the drop height are all variables.
terms.art: Four labelled sliders for wing length, paper, clip and height beside a paper spinner.

terms.meaning: The one variable you choose to change on purpose, to see what it does. Scientists call it the independent variable.
terms.example: In the spinner test, the thing you change is the length of the wings.
terms.art: A hand cutting three different wing lengths from the same strip of paper.

terms.meaning: The result you record, with a number and a unit. Scientists call it the dependent variable, because it depends on what you changed.
terms.example: In the spinner test, you measure the time in seconds that each spinner takes to fall.
terms.art: A phone stopwatch showing 1.5 seconds beside a falling spinner.

terms.term: The things you keep the same
terms.meaning: All the other variables, which you hold steady so they cannot change the result. Scientists call them control variables.
terms.example: Same paper, same clip, same drop height, same person dropping, and the fan switched off.
terms.art: A checklist with ticks next to paper, clip, height, dropper and fan.

terms.meaning: A number and a unit that tells how much of something there is.
terms.example: The spinner took 1.5 seconds to fall. The 1.5 is the number and seconds is the unit.
terms.art: A tape measure and a stopwatch side by side with their readings.

terms.meaning: One go at the test.
terms.example: Dropping a spinner once and timing it is one trial.
terms.art: A single spinner leaving a hand with the label trial 1.

terms.meaning: To do the test again in the same way, to see how much the results change.
terms.example: Drop each spinner five times, not once.
terms.art: Five spinners of the same kind falling one after another in a row.

terms.meaning: The typical size of a set of numbers. To find the average, add the numbers and divide by how many there are. Scientists also call it the mean.
terms.example: The times 14, 16, 15, 13 and 17 tenths of a second add up to 75. Divide by 5 to get an average of 15 tenths.
terms.art: Five numbers on a seesaw balancing at the middle point.

terms.meaning: How far a set of numbers spreads, from the smallest to the biggest. To find it, take the smallest from the biggest.
terms.example: For the times 13 to 17 tenths, the range is 17 take away 13, which is 4 tenths.
terms.art: A line with the smallest and biggest numbers marked and a bracket between them.

terms.meaning: A result that is far from all the others. Scientists also call it an outlier.
terms.example: Four drops took about 15 tenths and one took 28 tenths. The 28 is an odd result.
terms.art: A row of dots on a number line with one dot far from the others.

terms.meaning: A test is reliable if you get about the same results each time you repeat it.
terms.example: If five drops of a spinner all take close to 15 tenths, the test is reliable.
terms.art: Five arrows landing close together on a target.

terms.meaning: A test is valid if it really measures what your question asks about, and not something else.
terms.example: Timing how long a spinner takes to fall measures the fall, but not how pretty it is, so it would not answer a question about beauty.
terms.art: A ruler measuring a spinner's fall time, with a tick mark.

terms.meaning: What you decide from your results, written so that it says no more than the results show.
terms.example: In our drops, the spinner with the longer wings fell more slowly on average.
terms.art: A notebook page with the word conclusion and two lines written under it.

terms.meaning: A claim is what you say is true. Evidence is the numbers or things you saw that support it. Reasoning is why the evidence supports the claim.
terms.example: Claim: longer wings fall slower. Evidence: average 21 tenths against 12. Reasoning: bigger wings catch more air.
terms.art: Three boxes in a row labelled claim, evidence and reasoning with arrows between them.

terms.meaning: A graph that joins points to show how a measurement changes as the thing you change gets bigger or smaller.
terms.example: A line graph of wing length and average fall time shows the time going up as the wings get longer.
terms.art: A graph with wing length along the bottom and fall time up the side with a rising line.

terms.meaning: The part of any result that comes from luck and small changes you cannot control.
terms.example: A coin tossed ten times might give 4 heads one time and 7 heads another time, by chance.
terms.art: A coin spinning in the air with three question marks.

terms.meaning: A cause is something that makes something else happen. A fair test can show a cause. A pattern alone cannot.
terms.example: Longer wings catch more air, which makes the spinner fall more slowly. This is a cause.
terms.art: A row of dominoes with the first one falling and pushing the next.

terms.meaning: A leaning that pushes your results one way, such as hoping a certain answer is true.
terms.example: A person who hopes the long wings are slowest may stop the stopwatch a little late on those drops.
terms.art: A finger pushing on one side of a weighing scale.

terms.meaning: A test in which the person measuring does not know which thing they are measuring, so hope cannot bend the result.
terms.example: A helper times the drops without being told which wing length each spinner has.
terms.art: A helper with a blindfold holding a stopwatch and a spinner hidden in a bag.

terms.meaning: The push of air against something moving through it. Bigger flat surfaces get more air resistance.
terms.example: A spinner with big wings feels more air resistance, so it falls more slowly.
terms.art: A spinner falling with arrows pushing up from the air against its wings.

explanations.concept: The three jobs in every test
explanations.definition: Every fair test has three jobs. There is one thing you change, one thing you measure, and a list of things you keep the same.
explanations.description: Say you want to know whether a longer wing makes a paper spinner fall more slowly. The thing you change is the wing length. The thing you measure is the time it takes to fall, in seconds. The things you keep the same are the paper, the clip, the height you drop from, the person who drops it and the stopwatch person. Scientists call these the independent variable, the dependent variable and the control variables. You do not need the long names, but you do need the three jobs. A test with two things changing is a test in which you cannot tell which one made the difference. A test with nothing measured gives no results. A test with a loose list of things to keep the same lets hidden differences slip in.
examples: Question: does more salt in water make a potato float? Change: the amount of salt. Measure: whether the potato floats. Same: the potato piece, the glass, the amount of water.
Question: does a longer rubber band shoot a paper ball farther? Change: the length of the band. Measure: the distance. Same: the ball, the pull-back and the person.
Question: does the amount of water change how many seeds sprout? Change: the amount of water. Measure: the number of seeds that sprout. Same: the kind of seed, the plate, the warmth.
explanations.art: A table with three rows headed change, measure and keep the same, filled in for a spinner test.

explanations.definition: When you test an amount, such as a length or a temperature, try at least three settings. Three show you the shape of the pattern. Two cannot.
explanations.description: Suppose you test two wing lengths and the longer one falls slower. That is something. But you do not know whether the time rises steadily, or jumps and then stays flat. With three or four wing lengths you can see a shape. Does the time rise in even steps? Does it rise and then level off? Does it do something surprising in the middle? Three settings also give you a check on yourself. If the short and long wings differ but the middle one falls fastest of all, something odd is happening and you should look closer. Try to choose settings that are spread out evenly, such as 4, 6 and 8 centimetres.
examples: Test wing lengths of 4, 6 and 8 centimetres, not only 4 and 8.
Test 0, 1 and 3 teaspoons of water on seeds, not only none and plenty.
Test paper bridges with 0, 2 and 4 pleats to see how the strength grows.
explanations.art: A line graph with three points joined, next to a graph with only two points, and a question mark between them.

explanations.concept: Why the same test gives different numbers
explanations.definition: Even a careful test gives slightly different numbers each time. The wobble comes from small changes you cannot control, and from small slips in measuring.
explanations.description: A spinner dropped five times will never fall in exactly the same way. A draught moves the air a little. The hand lets go a little differently. The spinner starts a bit tilted. And the person with the stopwatch presses the button a fraction early or late. Human reaction takes about a fifth to a quarter of a second. These small changes add up to a wobble in the numbers. The wobble is not a mistake. It is part of any real measurement. Because of it, one number from one try is never the whole story. We need several tries to see what is steady and what is wobble.
examples: Dropping the same spinner five times gives times such as 1.4, 1.6, 1.5, 1.3 and 1.7 seconds.
Two people measure the same table and get 120 and 122 centimetres.
A cricketer bowling the same ball ten times will not land it on exactly the same spot.
explanations.art: Five slightly different paths of a spinner falling, drawn as five faint lines from the same hand.

explanations.definition: Repeat each setting several times, add up the results and divide by the number of tries. This gives the average, which is steadier than any single try.
explanations.description: One try can be unusually high or unusually low. When you repeat the test, the highs and lows pull against each other. The average sits in the middle. To find it, add the numbers and divide by how many there are. If the spinner took 14, 16, 15, 13 and 17 tenths of a second, the sum is 75. Divide by 5. The average is 15 tenths, or 1.5 seconds. Averages are also useful for comparing: if one spinner averages 1.5 seconds and another averages 1.9 seconds, we can compare them more fairly than by looking at one drop each. But an average alone hides how much the numbers spread, so we also look at the range.
examples: Five drops: 14, 16, 15, 13, 17 tenths. Total 75, average 15.
Three bridges held 8, 10 and 9 coins. Total 27, average 9.
Rainfall in a week, measured daily, is averaged to show a typical day.
explanations.art: Five bars of different heights with a dotted horizontal line across them at the average.

explanations.concept: The range: how far the numbers spread
explanations.definition: The range is the biggest number minus the smallest. It shows how much the numbers wobble.
explanations.description: Two sets of numbers can have the same average and be very different. One set could be 15, 15, 15, 15, 15. Another could be 5, 10, 15, 20, 25. Both average 15. The first is steady and the second is all over the place. The range shows the difference: 0 and 20. When we compare two spinners, the range tells us how much to trust the difference between their averages. If one averages 15 and another 19, and each has a range of 4, the difference of 4 is about the same as the wobble. We would want more tries. If their ranges are 1, the difference of 4 is clear.
examples: Times 14, 16, 15, 13, 17 tenths have a range of 4 tenths.
Coins held: 8, 10, 9. The range is 2.
Two bowlers with the same average speed can have very different ranges.
explanations.art: Two dot graphs with the same middle point, one with tight dots and one with spread-out dots.

explanations.concept: The odd result: check, do not hide
explanations.definition: An odd result is far from all the others. Check how the test was done and repeat it. Do not rub it out, and do not use it without thinking.
explanations.description: In five drops of a spinner, four take about 15 tenths and one takes 28 tenths. What happened? Perhaps the spinner clipped the wall. Perhaps the timer stopped late. Perhaps a draught caught it. First, ask whether something went wrong that you can name. If so, write that down, and drop it again. If you cannot find a reason, keep the result, and do more tries. A result that appears again is real. A result that appears once may be a fluke. Never delete an odd result in secret. Many discoveries began as a strange number that someone kept and looked at again.
examples: Four drops take about 15 tenths and one takes 28. Check for a bump and drop again.
One bridge holds 31 coins when the others hold about 11. Check if that bridge was folded differently.
One of ten tomato plants grows twice as tall as the others. Look at the pot, the soil and the light before deciding.
explanations.art: A row of dots on a number line with one far dot circled and a magnifying glass over it.

explanations.description: Teachers often say three repeats, and five is better. But the right number depends on how big the wobble is compared with the difference you are looking for. If the wobble is small, three tries may do. If the wobble is large, you need many more. Nobody has a number that is right for every test. Scientists decide before they start, and they say how many they used.
examples: Three drops of a spinner are quick, but five show the wobble better.
Weighing a coin ten times on a kitchen scale shows the scale's wobble clearly.
Medicine trials use thousands of people, because the differences are small compared with how people vary.
explanations.art: A pile of ten balls beside a scale with a question mark asking how many are enough.

perspectives.explanation: Three repeats are a simple rule that children can manage, and it is enough to show whether a result is steady or not. Doing more may take too long.
No single number is right. How many repeats you need depends on how big the wobble is and how small a difference matters. A test with a large wobble needs many tries to be trusted.

explanations.definition: When we hope for a particular result, small choices in measuring can lean towards it without us noticing. A blind test, in which the measurer does not know which thing is which, helps.
explanations.description: Suppose you hope the long-winged spinner is slowest. You may release it a little more gently, and you may stop the timer a little later. You are not cheating on purpose. This is how our minds work. To protect a test from this, scientists often use a blind test. A helper times the drops without knowing which wing length each spinner has. Or the spinners are labelled with secret letters. Another habit is to write down what you expect before the test, so that you can see afterwards whether your hopes and your result matched.
examples: A helper times the drops while the spinners are hidden in a bag and labelled with letters.
Drug trials often keep doctors and patients from knowing who has the real medicine.
A judge in a talent show who hears singers from behind a curtain cannot be pushed by how they look.
explanations.art: A helper holding a stopwatch with a spinner hidden behind a curtain labelled with a letter.

explanations.concept: Tables, bar charts and line graphs
explanations.definition: A table keeps every number in place. A bar chart compares separate things. A line graph shows how a result changes as an amount changes.
explanations.description: Start every test with a table, ready before you begin. Put the thing you change in the first column, and your trials and averages in the next columns. Use a bar chart when the things you compare are separate, such as four different bridge shapes. Use a line graph when the thing you change is an amount that can sit anywhere along a line, such as wing length or amount of water. A line graph shows the shape, such as a steady rise, a levelling off or a dip. Label both sides with what they show and the units, and give the chart a title. Plot averages, not single tries, and write the range next to each point if you can.
examples: A bar chart for four bridge shapes: flat, channel, pleated and tube.
A line graph for wing lengths 4, 6 and 8 centimetres against average fall time.
A table with a column for each trial and extra columns for the average and range.
explanations.art: A bar chart of four bridges on the left and a line graph of three wing lengths on the right.

explanations.concept: Writing a conclusion that says no more than you found
explanations.definition: A good conclusion has a claim, evidence and reasoning. It says what you found in your test, with its limits, and does not claim more.
explanations.description: A claim answers your question. Evidence gives the numbers that support it. Reasoning explains why the numbers support the claim. A good conclusion also has limits. It says what you tested and does not go beyond. If you tested three wing lengths, you can say what happened for those three. You cannot say what happens for a wing of 20 centimetres. If you measured on one day in one room, say that. Use careful words such as 'in our test', 'on average' and 'the evidence suggests'. If your results are not clear, say 'we cannot tell yet' and say what you would do next.
examples: Claim: longer wings fell more slowly. Evidence: the average time rose from 12 to 16 to 21 tenths. Reasoning: bigger wings catch more air. Limit: we tested only 4, 6 and 8 centimetres.
Claim: in our two weeks, we could not tell whether tulsi changes the mosquito count. Evidence: a difference of about one a night, smaller than the swings.
Claim: the pleated bridge held the most. Evidence: an average of 24 coins against 6 for the flat one.
explanations.art: A notebook page with three boxes labelled claim, evidence and reasoning, and a small note beside it marked limits.

explanations.definition: A difference between two sets of results may come from a real cause, from chance, or from a hidden difference in the test. Repeating and comparing the wobble helps tell which.
explanations.description: When two things come out differently, there are three possible reasons. First, the thing you changed really did it. Second, chance made a difference, as when a coin gives 7 heads one time and 4 the next. Third, something else was different that you did not notice. A fair test removes the third. Repeating and looking at the range deals with the second. If the difference between two averages is bigger than the wobble in each, chance is an unlikely reason. If the difference is smaller than the wobble, you cannot say. Finally, a pattern in a table does not by itself say that one thing makes the other. A fair test, or other careful evidence, is needed for that.
examples: Two identical plates of seeds gave 7 and 9 sprouted seeds. A difference of 2 can come from chance alone.
A tulsi corner had about one mosquito fewer a night, but nights varied from 2 to 9. The difference is smaller than the wobble.
Children with big shoes read better, but age lies behind both.
explanations.art: Three branching arrows from a difference in results labelled real cause, chance and hidden difference.

explanations.concept: Why a longer wing slows a spinner
explanations.definition: A spinner falls because gravity pulls it down. The air pushes back against its wings. Bigger wings meet more air, so the push is bigger and the spinner falls more slowly.
explanations.description: When the spinner falls, its wings spin like the blades of a helicopter. The spinning wings sweep through the air. The air pushes up against them, and this push is called air resistance. A bigger wing has more surface to push against, so the push is stronger. The spinner speeds up until the push of the air equals its weight. After that it falls at a steady speed. Bigger wings reach that balance at a slower speed. The paper and the clip weigh the same whatever the wing length, so only the wings differ. This is why seeds of maple trees, which have long wings, spin slowly to the ground and can travel a long way on the wind.
examples: A flat sheet of paper falls more slowly than the same sheet crumpled into a ball.
A parachute is a very big wing for its weight, so it falls slowly.
Maple seeds spin down on a single wing and drift far from the tree.
explanations.art: A paper spinner with arrows pushing upward from the air against its spinning wings and a downward arrow for its weight.

explanations.concept: Why a fold makes paper strong
explanations.definition: A flat strip of paper bends easily. A fold, a pleat or a tube puts the paper further from the middle line of the bend, and that makes it much stiffer.
explanations.description: Try bending a flat strip of paper across a gap. It sags at once. Fold two edges up to make a channel, and it holds far more. When a strip bends, the top side is squeezed and the bottom side is stretched. The paper in the middle does very little. A fold puts more paper at the top and the bottom, away from the middle, where it can do the most work. A tube or a pleated sheet does this very well. The same idea explains why steel girders are shaped like the letter I, and why bamboo is hollow. Engineers say that the shape matters as much as the material.
examples: A rolled newspaper can hold a heavy book, though a flat sheet cannot.
Corrugated cardboard has pleats inside, which make it stiff for its weight.
Bamboo and many plant stems are hollow tubes, which are stiff for their weight.
explanations.art: Side view of a flat strip sagging and a pleated strip staying straight between two stacks of books.

agreed.text: Repeating a measurement gives slightly different numbers each time, and this wobble is a normal part of measuring.
agreed.evidence: Anyone who times the same spinner five times, or weighs the same coin ten times, sees the numbers differ a little.

agreed.text: The average of several tries is steadier than any one try, and the range shows how far the numbers spread.
agreed.evidence: Averages of repeated tries vary much less than single tries. This has been shown in countless measurements, from school timings to physics experiments.

agreed.text: When you test an amount, trying at least three settings shows the shape of the pattern better than two.
agreed.evidence: Two points can be joined by a straight line however the real result behaves. A third point can show a bend or a levelling off.

agreed.text: An odd result should be checked and repeated, and recorded, and never quietly deleted.
agreed.evidence: Scientific societies treat hiding results as a serious fault. Some important discoveries began as an odd result that someone kept.

agreed.text: A conclusion should say no more than the results show.
agreed.evidence: Scientists who study how well results can be repeated have found that results stated too strongly often do not hold up in later tests.

agreed.text: A difference between two averages is only worth trusting if it is bigger than the wobble within each set of results.
agreed.evidence: This is the basic idea behind the statistical tests that scientists use to tell a real difference from chance.

challenging.claim: If I get the same answer once, I know it is right.
challenging.for: A clear result feels convincing, and some differences are so large that one try shows them.
challenging.against: One try can be a fluke, or a slip of the stopwatch. Repeating shows whether the result stays the same. A result that comes only once cannot be trusted much.

challenging.claim: Averages hide the truth, so scientists should only look at single results.
challenging.for: An average does hide how much the results spread.
challenging.against: That is why scientists report the range as well. A set of numbers described by both the average and the range is more honest than one lucky try.

challenging.claim: An odd result is a mistake, so delete it.
challenging.for: Sometimes an odd result is a slip, such as a bump or a late stopwatch.
challenging.against: Only checking can show whether it is a slip. If you cannot find a reason, it might be real. Deleting an odd result in secret hides what could be the most interesting part of the test.

challenging.for: Three is quick, and it shows a rough spread.
challenging.against: When the wobble is large compared with the difference you are testing, three repeats are not enough. Scientists decide on the number of repeats according to the size of the wobble.

challenging.claim: If I keep everything the same except one thing, my test is perfect.
challenging.who: Many people who learn about fair tests.
challenging.for: Keeping everything else the same is the heart of a fair test.
challenging.against: No test keeps everything the same. Two paper strips are never exactly alike, and the air always moves a little. A good test keeps the important things the same, repeats the test, and says what was not controlled.

challenging.claim: A good scientist has no hopes and no guesses.
challenging.for: Hopes can bend the results, so it seems best to have none.
challenging.against: Scientists do have hopes and guesses, and they cannot help it. What matters is how they protect the test from them, by writing predictions first, using blind tests and sharing their numbers for others to check.

challenging.claim: Real science only counts when a number comes out.
challenging.for: Numbers make comparing easy and clear.
challenging.against: Many careful tests produce words, drawings or counts, such as which seeds sprouted. What matters is that the observations are made carefully and recorded honestly.

big_questions.q: Nothing was changed, and yet the same spinner took a different time on each drop. Where did the difference come from?
big_questions.hint: Think about the air, your hand, the spinner's tilt and the person with the stopwatch.

big_questions.q: Is it possible to do exactly the same thing twice?
big_questions.hint: Think about the position of every particle of air in the room. Could it be the same twice?

big_questions.q: If the wobble in the numbers is as big as the difference you are testing, what should you do?
big_questions.hint: Think about more repeats, a bigger change, or a better way of measuring.

big_questions.q: A medicine test can be repeated with thousands of people. Why is that sometimes worth the cost?
big_questions.hint: Think about how different people are, and how small the effect of a medicine can be.

big_questions.q: You hope your idea is right. How can you test it so that your hope does not bend the result?
big_questions.hint: Think about writing your prediction first, a helper who does not know which is which, and sharing your numbers.

big_questions.q: If a scientist deletes an odd result in secret, who is harmed?
big_questions.hint: Think about the people who read the study, and the people who might have made a discovery from that number.

big_questions.q: Tu Youyou found that one hidden thing, how hot the plant was heated, decided whether the medicine worked. What hidden things might be changing your results?
big_questions.hint: Think about the room, the person, the time of day and the paper.

big_questions.q: When you cannot repeat something, such as an eclipse or a monsoon, how can you still be careful?
big_questions.hint: Think about comparing many different events and recording exactly what was seen.

big_questions.q: Who decides what counts as a difference that matters?
big_questions.hint: Think about a difference of half a second in a sprint and in a snail race.

story.title: The Mosquitoes and the Tulsi
story.note: A made-up story. The science in it is real: one count is one throw of the dice, and a difference needs to be bigger than the night-to-night wobble before we trust it. The flat, the counts and the tulsi test are imagined, and the story does not say whether tulsi keeps mosquitoes away.
text: Aadhira lived in a flat in Kozhikode with her mother, her father and her Appooppan, her grandfather. Appooppan loved plants more than anything. On the balcony he kept a big pot of tulsi, with soft green leaves that smelled sharp and sweet.
"A tulsi near the window keeps the mosquitoes out," Appooppan always said. "In all my years, I have never been wrong about this."
Aadhira loved her grandfather, and she loved asking questions. One evening, while the mosquitoes whined around the lamp, she asked, "Appooppan, how do you know?"
He laughed. "Because I have always known."
"That is not the same," said Aadhira, and she went to find her notebook.

The balcony had two corners. Aadhira stuck a white card on the wall of each corner, at the height of her shoulder. The tulsi pot stood in the left corner. The right corner had nothing. "Tonight," she said, "I will count the mosquitoes that settle on each card in the ten minutes after the lights come on. I will keep everything else the same."
Appooppan crossed his arms. "You will see."
The first evening, Aadhira held the timer and counted. The tulsi corner had 2 mosquitoes. The empty corner had 9.
"See!" cried Appooppan, thumping the arm of his chair. "Two and nine! What did I tell you?"

Aadhira looked at the numbers. She felt a small pleasure too, because she liked a clear answer. But she also remembered something from school. She took a breath. "That is one evening, Appooppan. It is like one throw of the dice. Let us see what the next evening says."
On the second evening the tulsi corner had 7 and the empty corner had 5. On the third it was 6 and 8.
Appooppan stopped thumping his chair. Aadhira frowned at her notebook. "I changed nothing," she said, "and the numbers jump around. Two, then seven, then six."
"The mosquitoes are cheating," said Appooppan.
"No," said Aadhira. "They are just not the same every evening. Nothing is. So one evening cannot tell us the answer. We need many."

Then she noticed another problem. The right corner was next to the door, where the whole family walked in and out. "Perhaps the empty corner gets more mosquitoes because of the door, and not because of the tulsi. I changed two things at once. The pot, and the place."
Appooppan stared at her. He had never heard a nine-year-old talk like that. "So what do we do?"
"We swap," said Aadhira. "Every second evening, you carry the tulsi to the other corner. Then each corner has the tulsi half the time. Whatever the door does, it does to both."
"I carry the pot?" said Appooppan, but he was already getting up.

For fourteen evenings they counted, and Appooppan carried the pot. Some evenings the tulsi corner had more. Some evenings it had fewer. The counts ran from 2 up to 9, and no pattern was clear. By the end Appooppan was counting too, whispering the numbers.
On the fifteenth morning, Aadhira added up. She wrote the totals at the bottom of the page. "With the tulsi, 71 mosquitoes in fourteen evenings. Without the tulsi, 84. The difference is 13."
"Thirteen!" said Appooppan. "That is something."

"It is about one mosquito a night," said Aadhira. "But look at the numbers. One evening it was 2 and the next it was 9. The nightly wobble is much bigger than that one mosquito. So I cannot be sure that the tulsi did anything."
Appooppan said nothing for a while. Then he said, very slowly, "So you are telling me that I might be right, and that you cannot tell."
"Yes," said Aadhira. "That is what the numbers say. Not more."

She wrote the conclusion in her notebook. In our balcony, over fourteen evenings, the tulsi corner had slightly fewer mosquitoes on average, about one a night. But the numbers swung much more than that, so we cannot say the tulsi keeps them away. We tested one pot of one size. We did not test a bigger plant.
Appooppan read it twice. "Hm," he said. "A bigger plant. Perhaps I should buy a bigger plant."
"Perhaps," said Aadhira, and she turned to a fresh page. "Then we will count again."

That evening, Appooppan took the timer himself. Aadhira noticed that he wrote the numbers down in the notebook, very neatly, in his old-fashioned handwriting. Under the numbers he wrote one new line. Tonight, 4 and 6. Who knows?
story.epiphany: One result is one throw of the dice. The same test gives different numbers each time, so only many tries show whether a difference is real or just wobble.
ask: Why did Aadhira not agree with her grandfather after the first evening?
What two things did Aadhira change at once at the start? How did she fix it?
Why did Aadhira say the difference of about one mosquito a night was not enough to be sure?
What could Aadhira and her grandfather do next to learn more?
Why did Aadhira write 'we did not test a bigger plant' in her conclusion?

games.title: Three Jobs: change, measure, keep the same
games.context: This is a card game about the three jobs in a test. Each card describes someone's test. You say what they change, what they measure and what they keep the same.

setup.art: Twenty test cards in a pile and a mat with three boxes headed change, measure and keep the same.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the cards and the mat. Shuffle the cards.

setup.art: A child reading a card aloud while the other players write three short answers on slips of paper.
setup.caption: 2. The reader reads a card. Everyone else writes down the three jobs.

setup.caption: 3. Compare your slips with the back of the card. Score points.

printables.title: 20 two-sided test cards: someone's test on the front, and the three jobs with a note on the back

items.f: Meenakshi asks: does idli batter rise higher in a warm place or a cool place? She puts the same batter in three cups. One goes in the fridge, one on the shelf, one near a sunny window. After six hours she measures how high each one rose.
items.b: Change: where the cup sits, which means how warm it is. Measure: how high the batter rose, in centimetres. Keep the same: the batter, the cup size, the amount of batter and the time.

items.f: Kavya asks: does a longer rubber band shoot a paper ball farther? She uses bands of 5, 10 and 15 centimetres. She pulls each back the same distance and measures where the ball lands.
items.b: Change: the length of the rubber band. Measure: how far the ball travelled. Keep the same: the ball, how far she pulled back, who shot it and the floor.

items.f: Arjun asks: does a wider paper plane glide farther? He makes planes with wings 4, 6 and 8 centimetres wide from the same paper. He throws each from one line in the same way.
items.b: Change: the width of the wings. Measure: how far each plane glided. Keep the same: the paper, the folds, the thrower, the line and the throw.

items.f: Lakshmi asks: does more water make more moong seeds sprout? Three plates of ten seeds get no water, one spoon or three spoons each morning. After three days she counts the seeds that sprouted.
items.b: Change: the amount of water. Measure: the number of seeds that sprouted. Keep the same: the kind of seed, the plate, the cloth, the warmth and the number of days.

items.f: Farhan asks: does a bigger coin sink faster? He drops a one, a two and a five rupee coin into a bucket from the same height and times how long each takes to reach the bottom.
items.b: Careful. The size and the weight change together, so this is not a clean test. Change: the coin. Measure: the sinking time. Fix: use things of the same weight but different sizes, such as a foil ball and a flat foil sheet.

items.f: Divya asks: does more sugar make tea taste sweeter? She puts 1, 2 and 3 spoons into cups of the same tea. A taster who knows which cup is which scores the sweetness from 1 to 10.
items.b: Change: the spoons of sugar. Measure: the sweetness score. Keep the same: the tea, the cup, the amount and the taster. Careful: the taster knows which cup is which, so hope could bend the score. A blind taster is better.

items.f: Sowmya asks: does a thicker straw let more juice through in ten seconds? She uses three straws of different widths and pours the juice into a cup. She measures the juice in the cup.
items.b: Change: the width of the straw. Measure: the amount of juice in ten seconds. Keep the same: the juice, the straw length, the height, the time and who sucks or pours.

items.f: Imran asks: do more rubber bands make a toy car shoot farther? He uses one, two and three bands on a launcher. He measures how far the car rolls each time.
items.b: Change: the number of rubber bands. Measure: the distance the car rolled. Keep the same: the car, the launcher, the floor and how far he pulls back.

items.f: Hetal asks: does a dark cloth get hotter in the sun than a light cloth? She lays a dark and a light cloth of the same size in the sun for ten minutes and reads a thermometer under each.
items.b: Change: the colour of the cloth. Measure: the temperature under it. Keep the same: the cloth size and type, the place, the time and the thermometer.

items.f: Nandini asks: how many pleats make a paper bridge hold the most coins? She tests strips with 0, 2 and 4 pleats and counts the coins each holds.
items.b: Change: the number of pleats. Measure: the number of coins held. Keep the same: the paper, the strip size, the gap and the way coins are added.

items.f: Mitali asks: does a stronger fan dry a wet cloth faster? She uses the low, medium and high settings for three cloths that are wet by the same amount. She times how long each takes to dry.
items.b: Change: the fan speed. Measure: the time to dry. Keep the same: the cloth, how wet it is, the distance from the fan and the room.

items.f: Shalini asks: does a longer string make a pendulum swing slower? She uses strings of 20, 40 and 60 centimetres and counts the swings in ten seconds.
items.b: Change: the length of the string. Measure: the number of swings in ten seconds. Keep the same: the weight, the starting push and the way she counts.

items.f: Ravi asks: how many spoons of salt does a potato piece need before it floats? He adds salt a spoon at a time to the same glass of water.
items.b: Change: the spoons of salt. Measure: whether the potato floats. Keep the same: the potato piece, the water, the glass and the stirring.

items.f: Anjali asks: do bigger leaves have longer stalks? She collects twelve leaves from the road and measures the leaf and the stalk of each.
items.b: This is a pattern search. She cannot change a leaf's size, so nothing is changed. Measure: leaf size and stalk length for each leaf. Keep the same: the way of measuring. Many leaves are needed to see a pattern.

items.f: Joseph asks: do more crows come to the balcony in the morning than in the evening? He counts crows for ten minutes at 7 am and at 6 pm for five days.
items.b: This is a long watch. He chooses the time of day but does not change the crows. Measure: the number of crows. Keep the same: the place, the length of each count and the way of counting.

items.f: Revathi asks: does warmer water dissolve sugar faster? She uses cold, room and warm tap water. She stirs each in the same way and times how long a spoon of sugar takes to vanish.
items.b: Change: the temperature of the water. Measure: the time for the sugar to vanish. Keep the same: the amount of water, the sugar, the stirring and the cup.

items.f: Zainab asks: does the size of a paper parachute change how fast it falls? She makes parachutes from squares of 10, 20 and 30 centimetres. Each has the same string and the same small weight.
items.b: Change: the size of the square. Measure: the time to fall. Keep the same: the string, the weight, the type of paper and the height of the drop.

items.f: Hari asks: do heavier balls bounce lower? He drops a marble, a tennis ball and a cricket ball from his shoulder and measures the bounce.
items.b: Careful. The weight, the size and the material all change at once, so this is not a clean test. Change: the ball. Measure: the bounce. Fix: compare balls that differ in only one way.

items.f: Kiran asks: does ghee or oil make a dosa crisper? He cooks one dosa with each. His brother scores the crispness from 1 to 5.
items.b: Change: ghee or oil. Measure: the crispness score. Keep the same: the batter, the pan, the heat and the time. Careful: one try each is not enough, so repeat the test.

items.f: Chitra asks: does a cloudy sky make the streetlight come on earlier? She writes the time it comes on each evening for a week and notes the clouds.
items.b: This is a long watch. She cannot change the clouds, so she watches for different kinds of evening. Measure: the time the light comes on. Keep the same: the light she watches and where she watches from.

printables.title: A mat with three boxes: change, measure, keep the same
A score sheet with one row for each player and 20 boxes

rules: One player is the reader. The reader takes the top card and reads the front aloud, but not the back.
Every other player writes three short answers on a slip of paper: what is changed, what is measured, and at least two things kept the same.
The reader reads the back. Each player scores 1 point for each job they got right, so up to 3 points.
Some cards have a trap. If a card has a trap, a player who spots it and says what is wrong or different wins 1 bonus point.
Pass the reader's job to the next player after each card. The game ends after 20 cards, or sooner if you want a shorter game.
The player with the most points wins. If you play alone, write your answers first and then check, and try to beat your own score.
If two answers are different but both sensible, the players can argue for theirs. A good reason keeps the point.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 20 cards and the mat. 2. Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile. 3. Give each player a pencil and some slips of paper.
flow.say: Every card is a test that someone planned. You say three things about it. What they change, what they measure, and what they keep the same.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Mix them up. Take a pencil and some slips.
flow.context: This is the first step of the game Three Jobs. You set up the cards and the mat.
flow.parent: If you cannot print, write each test on a strip of paper and keep the answers in a list.

flow.do: Read the first card as a practice. Ask your child to say the three jobs out loud before you read the back.
flow.say: Here is the first test. What is being changed? What is being measured? What must stay the same?
flow.kid: Read the first card. Say what is changed, what is measured and what stays the same.
flow.context: In this step, you play one practice card to learn how the game works.
flow.parent: Children often mix up the thing they change and the thing they measure. Ask: 'What did she choose to alter? What did she look at afterwards to see what happened?'

check.q: Kavya tests whether a longer rubber band shoots a paper ball farther. What is the thing she measures?
check.why: She changes the band length. What she measures is the result, which is how far the ball goes. The ball and the pull-back stay the same.

flow.do: Play the other 19 cards, or as many as the time allows. Take turns being the reader. The players write their slips first. Then the reader reads the back.
flow.say: Read the test. Everyone writes three jobs. Now turn the card over. Who has them right? Who spotted a trap?
flow.kid: Take turns. Read a test. Write the three jobs. Check the back.
flow.context: In this step, you play most of the cards. Watch for the traps.

ask.q: Which cards had a trap, and what was wrong?
good: Two things changed at once.
Only one try was made.
Nothing could be changed, so it was a pattern search.

flow.parent: The trap cards are about the heavier ball, the coins, the dosa and the leaves. Let your child spot what is wrong before you read the back.

flow.do: Add up the points. Ask which jobs were hardest to name. Ask what makes the 'keep the same' list hard to write.
flow.say: Let's count the points. Which job was the trickiest? Why is 'keep the same' the hardest list to write?
flow.kid: Add up your points. Which job was hardest? Why?
flow.context: In this step, you add up the points and talk about what was hardest.
flow.think: Pick a card where two answers could both be right. What would you check to decide?

games.title: Supported, Too Far, or Can't Tell Yet?
games.context: This is a card game about conclusions. Each card gives some results and a conclusion. You judge whether the conclusion is supported, goes too far, or cannot yet be told.

setup.art: Sixteen conclusion cards in a pile and three tokens in front of each player labelled supported, too far and can't tell yet.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the cards and the tokens. Shuffle the cards.

setup.art: A child reading a card with results and a conclusion while players put a token face down.
setup.caption: 2. Read the results and the conclusion. Pick a token.

setup.art: Players turning over their tokens together while the reader reads the back of the card.
setup.caption: 3. Turn over the tokens together. Read the back and score.

printables.title: 16 two-sided conclusion cards: results and a conclusion on the front, and the judgement with a reason on the back

items.f: Kavya dropped a spinner with 8 centimetre wings five times: 1.9, 2.1, 1.8, 2.0, 2.2 seconds. A spinner with 4 centimetre wings took 1.2, 1.1, 1.3, 1.2, 1.0 seconds. Her conclusion: in this test, the spinners with longer wings fell more slowly.
items.b: SUPPORTED. The averages are 2.0 and about 1.2 seconds, a gap of about 0.8. The numbers in each set spread by only about 0.4, so the gap is bigger than the wobble. She also says 'in this test', which is careful.

items.f: A blue pen and a red pen were each tried once on a rough page. The blue wrote 14 centimetres before it skipped, the red wrote 12. The conclusion: blue pens are better than red pens.
items.b: TOO FAR. It was one try each, with two particular pens. It says nothing about all blue pens. And the colour is not what was tested.

items.f: Ten moong seeds on a wet cloth: 10 sprouted. Ten moong seeds on a dry cloth: 0 sprouted. The conclusion: these moong seeds needed water to sprout.
items.b: SUPPORTED. The gap is as big as it can be, and the conclusion is limited to these seeds. This also matches what many people have seen.

items.f: A rubber ball bounced 40, 41 and 40 centimetres. A tennis ball bounced 35, 36 and 35. The conclusion: rubber balls bounce higher than any other ball.
items.b: TOO FAR. The test compared two balls. We cannot say 'any other ball' from it. A careful claim would say 'this rubber ball bounced higher than this tennis ball'.

items.f: In one class, the children with bigger shoes were taller. The conclusion: wearing bigger shoes makes children taller.
items.b: TOO FAR. This is a pattern, not a cause. Older children are taller and also have bigger feet. Age sits behind both.

items.f: Mosquito counts over 14 evenings: 71 with the tulsi pot and 84 without. Nightly counts ran from 2 to 9. The conclusion: tulsi keeps mosquitoes away.
items.b: CAN'T TELL YET. The difference of 13 over 14 nights is about one a night. The nightly numbers swing from 2 to 9, so the wobble is much bigger than the difference.

items.f: Plant A grew in sun, in a big pot of red soil, and reached 15 centimetres. Plant B grew in shade, in a small pot of black soil, and reached 12 centimetres. The conclusion: sunshine makes plants grow taller.
items.b: CAN'T TELL YET. The light, the soil and the pot all differ. Any of them could explain the gap.

items.f: Spinner times: 1.4, 1.5, 1.4, 1.6, 1.5 seconds. The conclusion: this spinner takes about 1.5 seconds to fall.
items.b: SUPPORTED. The times are close together, and the average is about 1.5 seconds. The word 'about' is honest.

items.f: Wings of 4 and 8 centimetres took 1.2 and 2.0 seconds. The conclusion: a wing of 6 centimetres will take exactly 1.6 seconds.
items.b: TOO FAR. A 6 centimetre wing was not tested. The time may be near 1.6, but we do not know. 'Exactly' goes much too far. We would have to test it.

items.f: A coin landed on heads 7 times in 10 tosses. The conclusion: this coin is unfair.
items.b: CAN'T TELL YET. A fair coin often gives 7 in 10 by chance. We would need many more tosses.

items.f: Bridge A held 12, 11 and 13 coins. Bridge B held 4, 5 and 4 coins. The conclusion: in this test, bridge A held more than bridge B.
items.b: SUPPORTED. The gap of about 7 coins is far bigger than the wobble of 2 within each set.

items.f: Five trials of one bridge held 10, 12, 11, 11 and 31 coins. The conclusion: this bridge holds about 15 coins.
items.b: CAN'T TELL YET. The 31 is an odd result that pulls the average up. Check that trial, repeat it, and then decide. Without it the average is about 11.

items.f: Sugar dissolved in 20 seconds in warm water and in 45 seconds in cold water. It was one try each. The conclusion: warm water dissolves sugar faster.
items.b: CAN'T TELL YET. The gap is large, so the idea is plausible, but one try each can be a fluke. Repeat the test a few times each.

items.f: A helper timed spinners and knew which was which, and hoped the long wings would be slowest. Long wings: 2.4, 2.5, 2.3, 2.4, 2.5 seconds. Short wings: 1.2, 1.1, 1.2, 1.2, 1.3 seconds. The conclusion: longer wings fell more slowly.
items.b: SUPPORTED. A hopeful helper might add a fifth of a second here or there. The gap is more than a second, so a small bias cannot explain it. A blind helper would still be better.

items.f: A girl measured arm span and height of six people. All were within 4 centimetres of each other. The conclusion: everyone in the world has an arm span within 4 centimetres of their height.
items.b: TOO FAR. Six people can only tell us about those six, and hint at a pattern for more. 'Everyone in the world' needs many more.

items.f: A streetlight came on between 6:05 and 6:15 pm on clear evenings and at 5:30 pm on the one cloudy evening. The conclusion: this light is switched by a light sensor.
items.b: CAN'T TELL YET. One cloudy evening is a good clue, but only one. Watch for more cloudy evenings before deciding.

printables.title: 12 tokens: four each of SUPPORTED, TOO FAR and CAN'T TELL YET
A score sheet with one row for each player and 16 boxes

rules: One player is the reader. The reader reads the results and the conclusion on the front, but not the back.
Everyone else takes three tokens, which are SUPPORTED, TOO FAR and CAN'T TELL YET. Each player puts one token face down.
Turn the tokens over together. The reader reads the back. A player scores 1 point for the right token.
A player who can say why also scores 1 more point. Compare the gap between the results with the wobble within each set.
Pass the reader's job to the next player. The game ends after 16 cards.
The player with the most points wins. If you play alone, choose a token before you check the back, and try to beat your own score.
Some cards can be argued both ways. A good reason keeps the point.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 16 cards and the 12 tokens. 2. Shuffle the cards. 3. Give each player three tokens, one of each kind.
flow.say: Each card gives some results and a conclusion. You decide if the conclusion is supported, goes too far, or cannot yet be told.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and tokens. Take three tokens, one of each kind.
flow.context: This is the first step of the game Supported, Too Far, or Can't Tell Yet. You set up the cards and the tokens.
flow.parent: If you cannot print, write the cards on strips of paper. Tokens can be three small bits of paper in three colours.

flow.do: Read the first card as a practice round. Ask your child to compare the gap between the two averages with the wobble in each set.
flow.say: Look at the two sets of times. How far apart are the averages? How far do the numbers wobble inside each set? Is the gap bigger than the wobble?
flow.kid: Read the first card. Is the gap bigger than the wobble?
flow.context: In this step, you play one practice card and learn to compare the gap with the wobble.
flow.parent: A simple rule for a child: if the gap between the averages is bigger than the spread within each set, the difference is probably real. If the gap is smaller, we cannot tell yet.

check.q: Two sets of times have averages of 2.0 and 1.2 seconds. Each set spreads by about 0.4. What does that suggest?
options: The gap is bigger than the wobble, so the difference is probably real
The gap is smaller than the wobble, so we cannot tell
check.why: A gap of 0.8 is twice the spread of 0.4 in each set. A gap bigger than the wobble is a good sign that the difference is real.

flow.do: Play the other 15 cards. Take turns being the reader. Say your reason aloud after you turn your token over.
flow.say: Read the results and the conclusion. Pick your token. Now turn them over together. Who can say why?
flow.kid: Take turns. Read a card. Pick a token. Say why.
flow.context: In this step, you play most of the cards and practise judging conclusions.

ask.q: What makes a conclusion go too far?
good: It says 'every' or 'always' from a few tries.
It says one thing causes another from a pattern.
It claims a number nobody tested.

flow.do: Add up the points. Choose the card that you found the hardest. Ask your child to rewrite its conclusion so that it says no more than the results show.
flow.say: Which card was hardest? Rewrite its conclusion so that it says only what the results show.
flow.kid: Pick the hardest card. Rewrite its conclusion.
flow.context: In this step, you add up the points and rewrite one conclusion.
flow.think: Good scientists would rather write a smaller true sentence than a bigger shaky one. Why?

experiments.title: The Paper Spinner: does a longer wing fall slower?
experiments.question: Does a paper spinner with longer wings fall more slowly? How much do the times wobble when you drop the same spinner again and again?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which spinner will fall slowest: short wings, middle wings or long wings? How much will the five times for the same spinner differ from each other? Why do you think so? Write your guess and your reason.
experiments.fair_test: The thing we change is the length of the wings: 4, 6 and 8 centimetres. The thing we measure is the time to fall from the same height, in seconds. We keep the same: the paper, the size of the strip, the paper clip, the person who drops, the person who times, the height and the room with the fan switched off. We drop the spinners in turns, short, middle, long, short, middle, long, so tiredness and draughts affect all three. We repeat each spinner five times.

materials.item: 3 strips of plain paper, each 4 centimetres wide and 16 centimetres long, all cut from the same sheet (ordinary notebook or printer paper)
3 paper clips of the same size
a ruler, a pencil and scissors
a phone stopwatch or a watch with a second hand
a sticky note to mark the drop height on the wall
a notebook and a pencil
a helper to drop the spinners, standing on the floor (a grown-up, because the drop is from about 2 metres up)

experiments.safety: Use scissors with a grown-up near. Keep the fan off. Stand on the floor, not on a chair, to drop the spinners. Paper clips are small parts: keep them away from children under five.
experiments.record: Fill in the results table. Work out the average and range for each wing length. Draw a line graph of average time against wing length.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you make three paper spinners with different wing lengths and drop each of them five times. You find out what changes the time and how much the time wobbles.

setup.art: A strip of paper 4 centimetres wide and 16 centimetres long with a cut line drawn down the middle from one end, marked 4, 6 or 8 centimetres.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a line down the middle from one end: 4, 6 or 8 centimetres long. Cut along the line.

setup.art: A paper spinner with the two wings folded in opposite directions and a paper clip on the bottom of the stem.
setup.caption: 2. Fold the two wings in opposite directions. Clip the bottom.

setup.art: A grown-up holding a spinner above head level beside a sticky note on the wall while a child holds a phone stopwatch.
setup.caption: 3. A helper drops the spinner from the sticky note mark. You time the fall.

setup.art: A table in a notebook with three rows of wing lengths and five columns for drops, an average and a range.
setup.caption: 4. Write each time in the table. Work out the average and range.

setup.art: A line graph with wing length along the bottom and average time up the side, with three points joined.
setup.caption: 5. Draw a line graph of the average time.

flow.do: Show your child the strips. Write three headings: Change, Measure, Keep the same. Ask your child to fill them in. Then ask for a guess and a reason. Also ask how much the five times for one spinner will differ.
flow.say: We will test spinners with different wing lengths. What do we change? What do we measure? What do we keep the same? Which spinner will fall slowest? How much will five times for the same spinner differ?
flow.kid: Fill in: change, measure, keep the same. Which spinner will fall slowest? Why?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Paper Spinner test. You plan the three jobs and guess.

ask.q: Which spinner will fall slowest, and why?
good: The one with the longest wings, because the air pushes them more.
The short wings, because they are lighter.
The middle, because it is just right.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Write both guesses at the top. The second guess, about how much the times will differ, is new. Let your child say a number, such as a quarter of a second. Roles: with one child, the child times and writes while you drop. With 2 to 4 children, one times, one writes in the table and one watches the spinner land and calls 'bumped' if it hits something. The dropper and the timer stay the same for all 15 drops, so the others can swap jobs only between spinners. Two children can also make their own set of three spinners and run them as a second set of drops, which gives you ten drops for each wing length.

check.q: In this test, which is the thing we change?
options: The time it takes to fall
check.why: We choose the wing length on purpose. The time is what we measure. The paper and the clip stay the same.

flow.do: 1. Cut three strips of paper 4 centimetres wide and 16 centimetres long. 2. On each strip, draw a line down the middle from one short end. Make the lines 4, 6 and 8 centimetres long. 3. Cut along the lines. 4. Fold the two flaps, which are the wings, in opposite directions. 5. Fold the bottom 1 centimetre of the stem up. 6. Clip a paper clip over the fold. 7. Write 4, 6 or 8 on each stem.
flow.say: Draw a line down the middle from the top, and cut it. That makes two wings. Fold one wing forward and one wing back. Fold the bottom up and clip it. Write the wing length on the stem.
flow.kid: Cut three strips. Cut the wings 4, 6 and 8 centimetres long. Fold the wings. Clip the bottom.
flow.context: In this step, you make the three spinners. They are alike in everything except the wing length.
flow.parent: The wings are each 2 centimetres wide. The stem gets shorter as the wings get longer, but the strip and the clip weigh the same for all three. If a spinner flutters or tumbles instead of spinning, bend the wings a little more apart and try again.

check.q: Why must the three strips and the three clips be the same?
options: So only the wing length is different
check.why: If the clips or the paper differed, the weight would change too. Then we could not tell whether the wings or the weight made the difference.

flow.do: Test each spinner once. Hold it at the sticky-note mark with the wings at the top and the clip at the bottom. Let go. Check that it spins and that all three spin. Mark the drop height with a sticky note on the wall.
flow.say: This is a practice drop. Let go, and watch the wings spin. Does each spinner spin as it falls? If one does not, we can bend its wings and try again.
flow.kid: Practise one drop with each spinner. Do they all spin? Do not time yet.
flow.context: In this step, you practise one drop each and fix any spinner that does not spin.
flow.parent: Mark the height on the wall with a sticky note at about the top of a grown-up's reach. The same grown-up drops every time, from the same mark, with the wings level and the arm stretched. Close the windows and switch off the fan. A spinner that will not spin is a real result. Write it down and try bending the wings a little.

flow.do: 1. The helper drops the spinners in turns: 4, 6, 8, 4, 6, 8, until each has been dropped five times. 2. The timer starts the stopwatch when the spinner leaves the hand and stops it when it touches the floor. 3. Write each time in the table to the nearest tenth of a second. 4. Do not rub out any time.
flow.say: Short, middle, long. Short, middle, long. Count 'ready, go' and start the timer when the spinner leaves the hand. Stop it when it lands. Write the time before the next drop.
flow.kid: Drop in turns: 4, 6, 8. Time each fall. Write every time down. Do not rub out.
flow.context: In this step, you drop and time each spinner five times, in turns.

ask.q: Why do we drop them in turns and not all five of one before the next?
good: So a draught or a tired arm affects all three spinners in the same way.
So no spinner gets an easier time.

flow.parent: Times from about 1 to 2.5 seconds are typical. If your spinners land in under a second, drop from a higher mark (a grown-up with an arm stretched up, standing on the floor), because a short fall makes the stopwatch error a big part of the time. The times for one spinner will differ by a few tenths of a second, which is the wobble. Reaction time at the stopwatch is about a fifth to a quarter of a second. Do not worry about this, and do not rub out a time that looks odd. Circle it instead. If a drop touches the wall or something else, write 'bumped' and drop again.
flow.wait: Take a short break after drop 8 if your arm or eyes get tired.

flow.do: 1. For each spinner, add up the five times. 2. Divide by 5 to find the average. 3. Take the smallest time from the biggest to find the range. 4. Circle any time that is far from the others.
flow.say: Add up the five times for the short wings. Divide by five. That is the average. Now the biggest minus the smallest. That is the range. Do the same for the other two.
flow.kid: Add the five times. Divide by five. Find the range. Circle any odd time.
flow.context: In this step, you work out the average and the range for each spinner.
flow.parent: To avoid decimals, you can use tenths of a second: 14, 16, 15, 13 and 17. The total is 75 and the average is 15 tenths. The range is 17 minus 13, which is 4 tenths.

check.q: Five times were 1.4, 1.6, 1.5, 1.3 and 1.7 seconds. What is the average?
check.why: The five times add up to 7.5. Divide by 5 to get 1.5 seconds. The 7.5 is the total, not the average.

flow.do: Ask your child to draw a line graph of the three averages against wing length, using the table. Then ask them to write a claim, evidence and reasoning, and one limit. Read the explanation 'Why a longer wing slows a spinner'.
flow.say: What can you say from your numbers? What is the claim? What is the evidence? Why does it happen? What can you not say?
flow.kid: What did you find? What is the evidence? Why? What can't you say?
flow.context: In this step, you draw a line graph and write a careful conclusion.

ask.q: What can you not say from your numbers?
good: What happens with a wing of 20 centimetres.
That it works for every kind of paper.
That a bigger wing always slows it by the same amount.

ask.q: Is the gap between the averages bigger than the wobble in each set?
good: Yes, so the difference is probably real.
No, so we cannot be sure yet.

flow.parent: A typical result is that longer wings give longer times, by a few tenths of a second or more, with times of about 1 to 2 seconds in all, but yours will differ and the order can even come out wrong for one pair. If the three averages are close together, say 'we cannot tell' and repeat with more drops or a bigger change in wing length.

experiments.title: The Paper Bridge: which fold holds the most coins?
experiments.question: A flat strip of paper sags at once. Which fold makes the strongest bridge: a channel with the edges folded up, a pleated fan, or a rolled tube? How many coins does each hold?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which shape will hold the most coins, and which the fewest? About how many coins will the flat strip hold? Why do you think so? Write your guess and your reason.
experiments.fair_test: The thing we change is the shape of the paper: flat, channel, pleated or tube. The thing we measure is the number of coins held before the bridge sags to the table. We keep the same: the paper and the strip size, the gap between the books, the overlap on each stack, the cup that holds the coins, and the way we add the coins, gently and one at a time. We use a fresh strip for each try, because a bent strip is weaker. We test each shape three times, in turns.

materials.item: 12 strips of the same paper, each 9.5 centimetres wide and 21 centimetres long, cut from 4 sheets of A4 paper
2 stacks of books of the same height, about 8 centimetres tall each, 15 centimetres apart
a small light cup, such as a paper tea cup or a small plastic curd cup (not a heavy steel katori)
about 60 coins of the same kind, such as one-rupee coins (borrow the family's loose change)
tape, a ruler and scissors
a notebook and a pencil

experiments.safety: Coins are small parts: keep them away from children under five, who might put them in their mouths. Do the test on a table, not on a shelf, so falling coins do not hit feet. Tape and scissors: a grown-up near.
experiments.record: Fill in the results table. Work out the average and the range for each shape. Draw a bar chart of the averages.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you fold paper into four bridge shapes and find out how many coins each can carry across a gap. You repeat each shape three times.

setup.art: Four paper strips side by side: one flat, one with the edges folded up into a channel, one folded into a fan of pleats, and one rolled into a tube.
setup.caption: 1. Fold the strips into four shapes: flat, channel, pleated and tube.

setup.art: A flat strip laid across a gap between two stacks of books, overlapping 3 centimetres on each stack, with a ruler showing the 15 centimetre gap.
setup.caption: 2. Lay a strip across the gap. Check the gap and the overlap.

setup.art: A small paper cup in the middle of a paper bridge being filled with coins one at a time by a child.
setup.caption: 3. Put the paper cup in the middle. Add coins one at a time.

setup.art: A bridge sagging and touching the table with a pile of coins in the cup and a hand writing a number.
setup.caption: 4. Stop when the bridge touches the table. Count the coins.

flow.do: Show your child the strips and the books. Ask for the three jobs in this test. Ask for a guess and a reason, and for a guess about how many coins the flat strip will hold.
flow.say: We will fold paper into four bridges. What do we change? What do we measure? What do we keep the same? Which will hold the most coins? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Four bridge shapes. Which holds the most? Which the least? Why?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Paper Bridge test. You plan and guess.

ask.q: Which bridge do you think will hold the most, and why?
good: The tube, because it is round and thick.
The pleats, because folding makes it thicker.
The channel, because the edges are like walls.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Write the guess and the reason at the top. If your child guesses a number for the flat strip, write it. Roles: with one child, you hold the strip steady and the child adds coins and counts. With 2 to 4 children, one adds coins, one counts aloud, one watches the middle of the bridge and calls 'stop', and one writes. Swap jobs after each shape. Two children can each build a set and test them, which gives you more tries for each shape.

flow.do: 1. Cut 12 strips of the same paper, each 9.5 centimetres wide and 21 centimetres long. 2. Leave 3 strips flat. 3. For 3 strips, fold the two long edges up by 2.5 centimetres to make a channel. 4. For 3 strips, fold the strip lengthwise like a paper fan, into pleats about 2 centimetres wide. 5. For 3 strips, roll the strip lengthwise into a tube about 3 centimetres across, and tape the seam. 6. Mark each strip with F, C, P or T.
flow.say: Three strips stay flat. Three get the edges folded up. Three become a fan. Three are rolled into tubes. Write the letter on each strip.
flow.kid: Cut 12 strips. Make 3 flat, 3 channels, 3 fans and 3 tubes. Write a letter on each.
flow.context: In this step, you make the twelve bridges. They are alike except for the shape.
flow.parent: All the strips are the same size before they are folded. The folds make them shorter in width. The tube must be rolled lengthwise, so it is 21 centimetres long. Stick the seam with a small piece of tape.

check.q: Why must all 12 strips be cut from the same kind of paper and be the same size?
options: So only the shape is different
So the bridges look the same
check.why: If the paper or the size differed, we could not tell whether the shape or the paper made the difference.

flow.do: Set up the two stacks of books with a gap of exactly 15 centimetres, measured with a ruler. Lay a flat strip across, with 3 centimetres on each stack. Place the cup in the middle. Practise adding one coin.
flow.say: The books are 15 centimetres apart. The strip rests 3 centimetres on each stack. The cup goes in the middle. Add one coin gently to see how it works.
flow.kid: Set the books 15 centimetres apart. Lay a strip across. Put the cup in the middle.
flow.context: In this step, you set up the gap and the cup, and practise adding a coin.
flow.parent: Keep the stacks of books the same height and the same gap for all tests. Measure the gap with a ruler each time you reset. The cup should sit in the middle and not touch the table. The stacks should be tall enough (about 8 centimetres) for a sagging bridge to be seen clearly. If a bridge slips off the books, tape the strip lightly to the top of each stack, the same way every time.

flow.do: 1. Test the shapes in turns: F, C, P, T, F, C, P, T, F, C, P, T. 2. Use a fresh strip each time. 3. Add coins to the cup, one at a time and gently. 4. Stop when the bridge touches the table, or falls, or after 60 coins. 5. Count the coins that were in the cup just before it failed. 6. Write the number in the table.
flow.say: Lay a fresh strip across. Add one coin at a time, gently. Keep going until the bridge touches the table. Count the coins in the cup just before it failed. Write the number down.
flow.kid: Test the shapes in turns. Add one coin at a time. Count the coins before the bridge touches the table.
flow.context: In this step, you test each shape three times, in turns, and count the coins.

ask.q: Why use a fresh strip each time?
good: A bent strip is weaker, so it would not be fair.
The first load might have squashed the folds.

ask.q: Why test in turns?
good: So any slow tiredness or change in the way you add coins affects every shape in the same way.

flow.parent: The flat strip usually holds very few coins, or none. If a shape carries all 60 coins without sagging to the table, write '60+' and treat it as a tie at the top. Then make the test harder by moving the stacks a little further apart (up to 17 centimetres, keeping 2 centimetres on each stack) and try again, or say honestly that you ran out of coins. All the numbers here are typical, not promised. The other shapes carry many more. Which is best may surprise you. Write what happens. If a bridge falls at once because it slid off the books, write 'slipped' and try a new strip. Do not rub out any result. If a number looks odd, circle it and try again with a fresh strip.

flow.do: For each shape, add up the three numbers and divide by 3 to find the average. Take the smallest from the biggest to find the range. Circle any number that is far from the other two.
flow.say: Add the three numbers for each shape. Divide by three. That is the average. Now the range, the biggest minus the smallest.
flow.kid: Find the average and the range for each shape.
flow.context: In this step, you work out the average and the range for each bridge shape.
flow.parent: If one of the three numbers for a shape is very different from the other two, test that shape two more times before deciding.

check.q: A shape held 9, 11 and 10 coins. What is its average?
check.why: The three numbers add up to 30. Divide by 3 to get 10. The 30 is the total, not the average.

flow.do: Ask your child to draw a bar chart of the four averages. Ask for a claim, evidence and reasoning. Ask what cannot be said. Read the explanation 'Why a fold makes paper strong'.
flow.say: What is your claim about the bridges? What numbers support it? Why does a fold make paper stronger? What can't you say from three tries?
flow.kid: Draw the bar chart. What did you find? What can't you say?
flow.context: In this step, you draw a bar chart and write a careful conclusion.

ask.q: What can't you say from your test?
good: That the same order holds for every kind of paper.
That it works over a longer gap.
That one shape is best for every job.

flow.parent: Typical results are that the flat strip holds almost nothing and the folded shapes hold many coins, with the tube and the pleats often best. Yours may differ. Honest results are the point. If the ranges overlap between two shapes, say 'we cannot tell which is better'.

activities.title: Measure the Table Ten Times: how much do numbers wobble?

materials.item: a table with a long straight edge
a ruler (a 30 centimetre ruler placed end to end works, but wobbles more), a tape measure or a string with a ruler
a notebook and a pencil
1 or more other people to measure, besides the child

schedule.what: Measure the same table edge many times. Work out the range and the average. Talk about the wobble.

activities.record: A list of every measurement, with the smallest, the biggest, the range and the average.
activities.context: In this activity, you measure the same table edge several times and see that the numbers differ a little. This is the wobble that makes repeating worth doing.

setup.art: A child laying a tape measure along the edge of a table and reading the number at the end.
setup.caption: 1. Measure one edge of the table to the nearest centimetre.

setup.art: Three family members each writing their own measurement on a slip of paper without showing it.
setup.caption: 2. Everyone else measures the same edge and writes their number secretly.

setup.art: A page with a row of different numbers for the table, with the smallest and the biggest circled.
setup.caption: 3. Put all the numbers in a row. Circle the smallest and the biggest.

flow.do: 1. Choose one straight edge of the table. 2. Your child measures it five times, to the nearest centimetre. They write each number on a new line without looking at the earlier ones. 3. Each other person measures it once and writes the number on a slip, without showing anyone. If you are only two, you measure five times too, without looking at your child's numbers. With 2 to 4 children, each child measures five times, so you have 10 to 20 numbers.
flow.say: Measure this edge of the table to the nearest centimetre. Write the number. Then do it again, as if it were the first time. Do you think all five numbers will be the same?
flow.kid: Measure the table edge five times. Write each number. Do not peek at the old ones.
flow.context: This is the first step of Measure the Table Ten Times. You measure the same edge again and again.

ask.q: Do you think all your numbers will be the same? Why?
good: Yes, because it is the same table.
No, because I might hold the tape differently.

flow.parent: Do not say what you expect. Let the numbers come out as they come. Ask your child to start the tape at the very end of the table each time.

flow.do: 1. Put all the numbers in a row, from smallest to biggest. 2. Find the range, which is the biggest minus the smallest. 3. Add all the numbers and divide by how many there are, to find the average. 4. Circle any number that is far from the rest.
flow.say: Put all the numbers in a row. What is the smallest? What is the biggest? How far apart are they? Now add them up and divide by how many there are.
flow.kid: Put the numbers in a row. Find the smallest and the biggest. Find the average.
flow.context: In this step, you work out the range and the average of your measurements.
flow.parent: Typically the numbers spread by about 1 to 3 centimetres on a table about a metre long, and more with a short ruler placed end to end. If someone is far out, ask how they held the tape. The average of many measurements is usually a better guess at the true length than any one.

check.q: Five measurements of a table are 120, 121, 120, 122 and 120 centimetres. What is the range?
