check.why: The biggest is 122 and the smallest is 120. 122 take away 120 is 2. The range tells us how much the numbers spread.

flow.do: Measure the same edge once with something else, such as a string or a hand span. Compare it with the ruler numbers. Ask which way of measuring gave a steadier answer.
flow.say: Now measure with your hand span, or a string. Is it the same as the ruler? Which way of measuring would you trust the most? Why?
flow.kid: Measure the edge with a string or a hand span. Which is steadier?
flow.context: In this step, you try a different way of measuring and compare the wobble.

ask.q: Which way of measuring gave the steadiest numbers, and why?
good: The ruler, because it has fixed marks.
The tape, because it bends around the edge.
The string, because I can mark the length.

flow.think: If a measurement can wobble by a centimetre, how big must a difference be before you trust it?

activities.title: The Sneaky Variable: spot what was not kept the same

materials.item: 2 small cloths of the same kind, such as handkerchiefs, one of them a little bigger than the other
a jug of water and a spoon
two places to hang them, one near a fan or a window and one in a corner
a notebook and a pencil

activities.safety: A grown-up switches the fan on and off.

schedule.what: A grown-up sets up a secretly unfair test. Your child finds what was different, and fixes it.

activities.record: A list of every difference you found, and a sentence saying how you would make the test fair.
activities.context: In this activity, a grown-up sets up an unfair cloth-drying test in secret, and you find all the differences that spoil it.

setup.art: Two cloths hanging in different places, one wet and one barely damp, one near a fan and one in a corner.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up sets up two cloths, with some differences that you cannot yet see.

setup.art: A child looking closely at the two cloths and writing a list of differences in a notebook.
setup.caption: 2. Look closely. Write every difference you find.

setup.art: The two cloths hanging in the same place, wet by the same amount, with a ruler between them.
setup.caption: 3. Make the test fair. Put both cloths in the same place and wet them the same.

flow.do: While your child is out of the room, wet one cloth with two spoonfuls of water and the other with one. Hang the first in the corner and the second near the fan. Use a cloth that is a bit bigger for one of them. Say that the test is to find which cloth dries faster.
flow.say: I have set up a test to find which cloth dries faster. I think there is something wrong with it. Can you find out what?
flow.kid: A grown-up sets up two cloths. Something is not fair. Wait until you are called in.
flow.context: This is the first step of The Sneaky Variable. A grown-up sets up the unfair test in secret.
flow.parent: Make three differences, not more: the amount of water, the place, and the size of the cloth. Do not tell your child how many. Keep the setup safe and dry underneath. With brothers and sisters, an older child can set it up for the others, with a grown-up checking the fan. Take turns.

flow.do: Ask your child to look at the two cloths and say every difference they can see. Write them down. Ask them to say which differences matter.
flow.say: Look closely at the two cloths. What is different about them? What else is different about where they hang? Write down every difference you find.
flow.kid: Look at both cloths. Write every difference you find.
flow.context: In this step, you look for the things that were not kept the same.

ask.q: What is different about the cloths and where they hang?
good: One is bigger.
One is wetter.
One is near the fan.
One is in a corner.

flow.parent: Some children find only the obvious difference. Prompt them with: 'What about the water? What about the size? What about where each one hangs?'

check.q: One cloth hangs near a fan and the other in a corner. The test is to find which cloth dries faster. What is wrong with this?
options: The place is different as well as the cloth
check.why: The fan could dry the first cloth faster, whatever the cloth is made of. When the place and the cloth both differ, we cannot tell which one made the difference.

flow.do: Now ask your child to say how they would make it fair. Fix the test. Wet both cloths the same, use the same size, and hang them side by side in the same place. You do not need to wait for them to dry. If you like, leave the unfair set-up and look again after an hour. Ask: did the first cloth dry first because of the cloth, the water, the size or the place? Nobody can say, and that is the point.
flow.say: How would you fix it? What do you keep the same? What is the one thing you change?
flow.kid: Fix the test. What stays the same? What is the one thing you change?
flow.context: In this step, you fix the unfair test and name the three jobs.

ask.q: What is the one thing you would change, and what would you measure?
good: The kind of cloth. I would time how long each takes to dry.
The place. I would time how long each takes to dry.

flow.think: A test with a hidden difference can look fair. How can you check your own tests for sneaky variables?

activities.title: Coin Wobble: how far can chance move a count?

materials.item: 1 coin
a notebook and a pencil
a family member or friend to toss too

activities.safety: Keep coins away from children under five.

schedule.what: Toss a coin ten times, five times over. Count heads each time. Look at how the counts spread.

activities.record: A table of five sets of ten tosses with the number of heads in each, the range and the average.
activities.context: In this activity, you toss one coin in sets of ten and see how much the count of heads wobbles by chance alone.

setup.art: A child tossing a coin onto a table with a tally of heads and tails written in a notebook.
setup.caption: 1. Toss a coin ten times. Make a tally of heads.

setup.art: A table in a notebook with five rows for five sets of ten tosses and a column for the number of heads.
setup.caption: 2. Do this five times and write the number of heads for each set.

setup.art: A row of five numbers on a page, with the smallest and the biggest circled.
setup.caption: 3. Find the range and the average of your five counts.

flow.do: Ask your child to guess how many heads they will get in ten tosses. Ask if they think the number will be the same each time they toss ten coins. Ask why.
flow.say: If you toss a coin ten times, how many heads will you get? Will you get that number every time you do ten tosses? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Toss ten times. How many heads? Will it be the same every set? Why?
flow.context: This is the first step of Coin Wobble. You guess before you toss.

ask.q: Will the count of heads be the same in each set of ten tosses?
good: No, because it is luck.
Yes, it should be five each time.
It will be near five but not always five.

flow.parent: Do not say anything about chance yet. Write the guess. Most children say five.

flow.do: 1. Toss the coin ten times and make a tally of the heads. 2. Write the number of heads for that set. 3. Do four more sets of ten tosses. 4. If another person is there, they do five sets too, and you can put all the sets side by side. With 2 to 4 children, each toss their own five sets with their own coin, or share one coin and take turns.
flow.say: Toss the coin ten times. Count the heads. Write the number. Do it again. We want five sets in all.
flow.kid: Toss ten times. Count the heads. Do it five times.
flow.context: In this step, you toss the coin and count the heads in five sets.
flow.parent: Typical counts are between 3 and 7, though a 2 or an 8 can happen. Do not worry if you get a 2 or an 8 now and then. That is chance too.
flow.wait: If you get tired, take a short break after set 3.

flow.do: Find the smallest and biggest count. Work out the range and the average. Ask whether any set was exactly five. Ask what this means for a test where one plate gets 3 sprouted seeds and another gets 6 out of 10.
flow.say: What was your smallest count of heads? What was your biggest? Was any set exactly five? If a coin can give 3 in one set and 7 in another, what does that mean for a test?
flow.kid: Find the smallest and the biggest. What does the wobble tell you?
flow.context: In this step, you look at how much chance moved the counts, and think about what that means for a test.

ask.q: What does the wobble in a coin tell you about a test with 10 seeds?
good: A difference of one or two seeds might be chance.
We need to repeat the test to be sure.

flow.think: If you tossed the coin 100 times in each set, would the counts wobble more or less in proportion?

check.q: Two identical plates of ten seeds, with the same water, gave 7 and 9 sprouted seeds. What is the best thing to say?
options: The difference of 2 can come from chance alone
The second plate got better water
The seeds in the first plate were weaker
check.why: Two plates treated the same way still differ, as two sets of coin tosses do. A difference of 2 between two single sets can be chance. We would need a bigger gap, or many more sets, to say a real cause is at work.

activities.title: From Table to Line: draw a line graph

materials.item: squared paper (graph paper or a graph notebook from a stationery shop, a few rupees) or plain paper with squares ruled lightly in pencil
a ruler and a pencil
your Paper Spinner averages, or the numbers in the activity

schedule.what: Draw the axes. Plot the averages. Join the points. Read the graph.

activities.record: A line graph with axes labelled and a title, and three sentences about what it shows.
activities.context: In this activity, you draw a line graph of the average fall time of a spinner against its wing length and read what the shape says.

setup.art: A page with two lines at right angles, labelled wing length across the bottom and fall time up the side.
setup.caption: 1. Draw two axes and label them with the units.

setup.art: Three dots on the graph at 4, 6 and 8 centimetres, joined by straight lines.
setup.caption: 2. Plot a dot for each average and join them.

setup.art: A finger running along the line to find a value for 5 centimetres between two points.
setup.caption: 3. Read the graph for a value in between.

flow.do: 1. Rule two lines at right angles on squared paper. 2. Label the line along the bottom 'Wing length (cm)' and mark 4, 6 and 8. 3. Label the line up the side 'Average fall time (tenths of a second)' and mark 0 up to 25. 4. Give the graph a title.
flow.say: Draw two lines. The one along the bottom is for what we change, the wing length. The one up the side is for what we measure, the time. Label both with units.
flow.kid: Draw two lines. Bottom: wing length. Side: fall time. Add units and a title.
flow.context: This is the first step of From Table to Line. You draw the axes.
flow.parent: If you did not do the Paper Spinner test, use these example averages: 4 centimetres gives 12 tenths of a second, 6 gives 16 and 8 gives 21. They are not from a real test, so say so on the graph. With 2 to 4 children, each child draws their own graph from the shared table, then compare.

flow.do: 1. Mark a dot for each average, at the right wing length and the right height. 2. Join the dots with a ruler. 3. If you know the range for each wing, draw a short vertical line through each dot to show it.
flow.say: Put a dot for each average. Join the dots with a ruler. If you know the range, draw a short line up and down through the dot to show how far the numbers spread.
flow.kid: Put a dot for each average. Join them. Draw the spread if you know it.
flow.context: In this step, you plot the averages and join them to make the line.

ask.q: What shape does the line make?
good: It goes up as the wings get longer.
It goes up faster after 6 centimetres.
It is nearly a straight line.

check.q: Why do we plot the average and not a single try?
options: The average is steadier than one try
The single try is always wrong
check.why: One try can be high or low by chance. The average of several tries is steadier, so the line shows the pattern more truly.

flow.do: Ask your child to put a finger on the graph where a wing of 5 centimetres would be. They read off a guess for the time. Ask whether a guess for 20 centimetres would be safe. Ask them to write three sentences about what the graph shows.
flow.say: Put your finger at 5 centimetres. What time do you think a spinner with 5 centimetre wings would take? Would a guess for 20 centimetres be safe? Why not?
flow.kid: Find 5 centimetres on the graph. What time do you guess? Is 20 centimetres a safe guess?
flow.context: In this step, you read a value between your points and think about guesses beyond them.

ask.q: Why is a guess for 20 centimetres less safe than a guess for 5?
good: I did not test anything near 20.
The line may bend or flatten out beyond 8.
5 is between points I tested, but 20 is far outside.

flow.think: A guess between two tested points is usually fairly safe. A guess far beyond the tested points is a much bigger gamble. Why?

projects.title: Thirsty Seeds: how much water do moong seeds need?

materials.item: 6 small steel katoris or saucers (small plates or lids will do), labelled A, B, C, D, E and F
kitchen tissue, a clean cotton cloth or a paper napkin, cut to fit each katori
60 whole moong seeds (green gram) from the kitchen, all unbroken and fresh from the same packet
a teaspoon and some water
a marker or sticky labels, a notebook and a pencil

projects.safety: Wash your hands after touching the seeds. Do not eat seeds that have grown mould or smell bad. Keep the katoris away from small children, who might put seeds in their mouths. If anyone in the family is allergic to moong or other pulses, use another seed or let someone else handle them.

schedule.what: Make the plan. Set up six katoris with ten seeds each. Add the first water.
Add the morning water. Look at each plate and note anything unusual.
Add the morning water. Count the sprouted seeds in each plate.
Count again. Work out the averages and ranges. Write the conclusion.

projects.record: A table with the six katoris, the water each gets, and the seeds sprouted on days 3 and 4. Under it, the average for each amount, the range, and a conclusion that says what you can and cannot say.
projects.context: In this project, you give three amounts of water to moong seeds, with two plates for each amount, and count how many sprout. You see how much chance moves the counts.

setup.art: Six steel katoris in two rows of three, each lined with tissue and holding ten moong seeds, with labels A to F.
setup.caption: 1. Set up six katoris with tissue and ten seeds in each.

setup.art: A hand adding one teaspoon of water to a katori while the others get none or three teaspoons.
setup.caption: 2. Give A and B no water. Give C and D one teaspoon. Give E and F three teaspoons.

setup.art: A close-up of a moong seed with a tiny white tail coming out, held by a pair of fingers.
setup.caption: 3. After three days, count a seed as sprouted when the white tail is at least 2 millimetres long.

flow.do: 1. Cut six pieces of tissue to fit the katoris. 2. Put one piece in each katori. 3. Count ten unbroken seeds onto each. 4. Label A and B for no water, C and D for one teaspoon, and E and F for three teaspoons. 5. Add the first water to C, D, E and F. 6. Put all six in the same place, away from sun and fan. 7. Write down the three jobs and your guess.
flow.say: We have three amounts of water: none, a little and plenty. Each amount gets two katoris, so we can see how much chance moves the counts. What do we change? What do we measure? What do we keep the same? Which katori will have the most sprouted seeds? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Set up six katoris. Two get none, two get a little, two get plenty. Which sprouts best? Why?
flow.context: This is day 1 of Thirsty Seeds. You plan the test and set up the katoris.

ask.q: What do we change, what do we measure, and what do we keep the same?
good: We change the water. We count the seeds that sprout. We keep the same seeds, katoris, tissue, warmth and number of days.

flow.parent: Use the same kind of seed from the same packet. Throw out cracked seeds. Keep the katoris side by side so the warmth is the same. Whatever you find is a real result. Before you begin, soak 5 seeds overnight: if they do not show a tail in 2 days, the packet is too old, so use another. Roles: with one child, the child sets up and you check. With 2 to 4 children, each looks after one amount of water (none, a little or plenty) and writes their own two katoris; the youngest counts the seeds out. If nothing sprouts even with plenty of water, the cause is old seeds or cold weather, so repeat in a warmer place. In hot, dry weather the one-teaspoon katoris can dry out by evening, so say so in your conclusion. Typically moong with plenty of water shows tails within 2 to 3 days, but your numbers will differ.

check.q: Why does each amount of water get two katoris?
options: So we can see how much chance moves the counts
So the seeds are not lonely
check.why: Two katoris treated the same way show how much the numbers wobble by chance. If they are very different, we know the wobble is large.

flow.do: Each morning for the next two days, add the water. Give C and D one teaspoon. Give E and F three teaspoons. Give A and B nothing. Look at all six katoris and write a few words about each. On day 3, count the sprouted seeds in each katori and write the numbers.
flow.say: Add the water as planned. A and B stay dry. Look closely at each katori. What do you see? Are any seeds changing?
flow.kid: Add the water. A and B get none. Look at each katori and write what you see.
flow.context: In these days, you water the katoris and look at the seeds.
flow.parent: Do not move the katoris between days. If mould grows on a seed, take the seed out and write that down. A seed that swells but has no tail is not yet sprouted.
flow.wait: Do this each morning for days 2 and 3. Then count on day 3 and again on day 4.

flow.do: On day 4, count the sprouted seeds in each katori. Work out the average and range for each amount of water. Write a claim, evidence and reasoning, with one limit.
flow.say: Count the sprouted seeds in each katori. A and B are one amount, so find their average. Do the same for C and D, and for E and F. What can you say? What can't you say?
flow.kid: Count the sprouted seeds. Find the average for each amount. What can you say? What can't you say?
flow.context: In this step, you count the seeds, work out the averages and write a careful conclusion.

ask.q: Is the difference between amounts bigger than the difference between two katoris with the same amount?
good: Yes, so the water probably made a difference.
No, so we cannot tell the two amounts apart yet.

flow.think: If you wanted to find a small difference between a little and plenty, what would you change in the test?

check.q: Katori C had 7 sprouted seeds and katori D had 9, both with one teaspoon. Katori E had 10 and F had 8, both with three teaspoons. What is the best thing to say?
options: We cannot tell whether one teaspoon and three teaspoons differ, because the two katoris with the same amount already differ by 2
Three teaspoons is better, because E had 10
One teaspoon is better, because D had 9
check.why: Two katoris with the same water already differ by 2 seeds. The gap between the two amounts is smaller than that. The difference between none and some water is probably bigger than that wobble.

challenges.title: Slowest Fall: engineer the slowest spinner and prove it
challenges.problem: Make a paper spinner that falls more slowly than your 6 centimetre-wing spinner. Then prove that it falls slower, using five drops of each and the average and range.
constraints: Use two equal pieces of the same paper, each no bigger than 10 centimetres by 20 centimetres, and two paper clips of the same size. Cut the baseline and the new design from these.
Tape is allowed, but no extra paper. Trim no more paper off one design than the other, or say how much you trimmed, so the weights stay nearly the same.
Drop both from the same mark on the wall, with the fan off.
Change only one thing at a time. Say which thing you changed.
Each design must be dropped at least five times.
materials: a phone stopwatch or a watch with a second hand
a baseline 6 centimetre-wing spinner, made again from one of the equal pieces of paper
general: Make the wings longer or wider. More wing area means more air resistance.
Fold the wings a little further apart, so they catch more air as they spin.
creative: Try tilting the wings at a different angle by bending them more or less, and see which angle gives the slowest fall.
Fold the tips of the wings a little to keep them stiff, so they do not droop as the spinner spins.
Try a very different shape, such as a single-winged spinner like a maple seed, and time that.
challenges.safety: Use scissors with a grown-up near. Stand on the floor, not on a chair, to drop the spinners. Keep the fan off. Paper clips are small parts: keep them away from children under five.
challenges.your_turn: Choose a different thing to slow down, such as a paper cup parachute or a leaf-shaped glider. Plan a test with the three jobs, repeat it five times, and show your averages and ranges.
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You improve a paper spinner by changing one thing at a time and prove it with repeated measurements.

setup.art: A child sketching three spinner designs on paper with different wing shapes, and circling one.
setup.caption: 1. Sketch ideas. Choose one thing to change.

setup.art: A helper dropping a baseline spinner and a new spinner from the same mark on the wall while a child holds a stopwatch.
setup.caption: 2. Drop the baseline five times and the new design five times.

setup.art: A notebook table with averages and ranges for the baseline and the new design side by side.
setup.caption: 3. Compare the averages with the ranges.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Ask your child to sketch two or three ideas. Ask which one thing they will change. Ask what they will keep the same.
flow.say: You need to beat your 6 centimetre spinner. What could make a spinner fall slower? Which one thing will you change first?
flow.kid: Sketch two ideas. Choose one thing to change first.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Slowest Fall challenge. You plan the design.

ask.q: What one thing will you change?
good: The length of the wings.
The width of the wings.
The angle of the wings.

flow.parent: If your child wants to change two things at once, ask: 'If it works, how will you know which one did it?' With 2 to 4 children, each child builds their own design and all of them compete against the same baseline, with one dropper and one timer. With one child, you can be the dropper.

flow.do: 1. Drop the baseline spinner five times and write each time. 2. Build the new design. 3. Test it once, to be sure it spins. 4. Drop it five times and write each time. 5. Drop in turns, baseline, new, baseline, new.
flow.say: First, the baseline. Five drops, five times. Then your new spinner. Five drops, five times. Drop in turns, so tiredness and draughts affect both.
flow.kid: Drop your old spinner five times. Then your new one. Write every time.
flow.context: In this step, you time the baseline and the new design, five drops each.
flow.parent: The same helper drops and the same timer times. Use the mark on the wall. Do not rub out any times. If one time looks odd, circle it, and drop again if you can see a reason, such as a bump.

flow.do: Work out the average and range for both designs. Ask whether the gap between the averages is bigger than the spread in each set. Ask for a claim, evidence and reasoning.
flow.say: What is the average for the old spinner? What is it for the new one? Is the gap bigger than the spread within each set? Can you prove your design is slower?
flow.kid: Find both averages and ranges. Is the gap bigger than the spread? Did you prove it?
flow.context: In this step, you compare the two designs honestly, using the averages and the ranges.

ask.q: What would you do if the gap is smaller than the spread?
good: Drop more times.
Make a bigger change to the wing.
Measure more carefully, for example with slow-motion video.

flow.parent: This is the fairest part of the challenge. Many first designs are only slightly different. A bigger change, such as doubling the wing area, shows up more clearly. A slow-motion phone video can time the fall more steadily than a stopwatch.

check.q: Old spinner averages 1.4 seconds with times from 1.2 to 1.6. New spinner averages 1.6 with times from 1.4 to 1.8. What is the best conclusion?
options: The gap of 0.2 is the same size as the spread, so it is too close to call
The new spinner is much slower
check.why: The gap between the averages is 0.2. The spread in each set is 0.4. The gap is smaller than the spread, so more drops, or a bigger change, are needed to be sure.

flow.do: Show the results to the family. Talk about what you would change next time. Write a conclusion that says what you proved and what you did not.
flow.say: Tell us what you tested, what you found, and what you could not prove. What would you try next?
flow.kid: Show your family your results. What did you prove? What would you try next?
flow.context: In this step, you share your results and write a careful conclusion.
flow.think: Which is better, a design that falls slowly once, or one that falls slowly every time? Why?

worksheets.title: The Three Jobs and the Wobble (core)

items.p: Arjun tests whether a thicker straw lets more juice through in ten seconds. What is the thing he changes?
opts: The amount of juice that passes
items.why: He chooses the straw on purpose. The amount of juice is what he measures, and the ten seconds is kept the same for every straw.

items.p: A girl tests whether more rubber bands make a toy car shoot farther. Sort each item into change, measure or keep the same.
items.why: The number of bands is what she chooses to alter. The distance is the result. Everything else stays steady so that only the bands can explain a difference.

items.p: If you repeat a test in exactly the same way, you will always get exactly the same number.
items.why: False. Small changes you cannot control, such as a draught or the timing of the stopwatch, make the numbers differ a little each time. This wobble is normal.

items.p: To find the average of a set of numbers, add them up and ____ by how many numbers there are.
items.why: Adding gives the total. Dividing the total by how many there are shares it out evenly, and that is the average.

items.p: Five spinner drops took 12, 14, 13, 15 and 16 tenths of a second. What is the average?
items.why: 12 plus 14 plus 13 plus 15 plus 16 is 70. 70 divided by 5 is 14. The 70 is the total, not the average.

items.p: The five times were 12, 14, 13, 15 and 16 tenths of a second. What is the range?
items.why: The biggest is 16 and the smallest is 12. 16 take away 12 is 4. The range shows how far the numbers spread.

items.p: Four drops of a paper spinner took about 15 tenths of a second, and one took 28 tenths. What should you do about the 28?
items.a: Look for a reason, such as a bump or a late stopwatch, and write it down. Drop the spinner again. If no reason is found and it happens again, keep it as a real result.
items.why: A strong answer checks and repeats before deciding, and does not rub out the number in secret.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
items.why: These words are used in every careful test. A strong answer could give an example of each.
pairs: Average
the typical size of a set of numbers, found by adding and dividing
Range
the biggest number minus the smallest
Odd result
a result far from all the others
Reliable
gives about the same results each time you repeat it
Conclusion
what you decide from your results, with its limits

items.p: Put the steps of a repeated test in a good order.
a: Write the three jobs and a guess
Make everything ready the same way
Test each setting in turns, several times
Work out the average and range for each setting
Write a conclusion with its limits
items.why: Plan and guess first, then prepare, then test in turns and repeat. Only then do the average and range, and only at the end the conclusion.
items: Work out the average and range for each setting
Write the three jobs and a guess
Write a conclusion with its limits
Test each setting in turns, several times
Make everything ready the same way

items.p: Three of these belong in a list of things to keep the same in a bridge test. Which is the odd one out?
opts: the size of the paper strip
the way the coins are added
items.why: The shape of the fold is the thing the test changes. The other three are kept the same.

items.p: Why do we test at least three wing lengths and not just two?
opts: Three settings show the shape of the pattern, such as a steady rise or a levelling off
items.why: With two points you can only draw a straight line between them. A third point can show a bend or a flat part.

items.p: An odd result should be rubbed out so the table looks neat.
items.why: False. An odd result may be a slip, or it may be real. Check it, repeat it and keep the record.

items.p: Draw a results table for testing three straw widths, with five drops each. Give it headings for the straw width, each try, the average and the range.
items.a: A table with a row for each of three straw widths. Columns headed Width (mm), Try 1 to Try 5 (ml), Average (ml) and Range (ml).
items.why: A strong table has headings with units, one row for each setting and room for every try, the average and the range.
items.art: An empty table in a notebook with three rows and eight columns, and a ruler beside it.

items.p: Which conclusion says no more than the results show?
opts: In our test, the pleated bridge held more coins than the flat one
Pleated bridges are the strongest bridges in the world
Folding paper always makes it stronger
items.why: The first sentence says what was tested and found. The others claim far more than three tries on one kind of paper can show.

items.p: Two cousins plan a test. One wants to repeat each setting 3 times. The other wants to repeat each setting 10 times. The test is quick. Who do you agree with?
items.a: A strong answer says the number depends on the size of the wobble and the time available. If the test is quick, more tries are better. Both cousins have a point.
items.why: Pick-a-side questions have no single right side. Marks go for using the idea of the wobble and for stating the other view fairly.

views.says: Three tries are enough to see whether the numbers stay close together. More tries take longer, and I might get bored and make mistakes.
Ten tries show the wobble far better. If the test is quick, there is no reason not to do more.

items.ask: How many repeats would you choose, and why?

items.p: Rewrite this conclusion so that it says no more than the results show: 'Paper bridge A is the best bridge in the world.' Bridge A held 12, 11 and 13 coins. Bridge B held 4, 5 and 4 coins.
items.a: In our test, bridge A held more coins than bridge B. It held an average of 12 coins and B held an average of about 4.
items.why: A strong answer says what was tested, names the numbers or the averages, and avoids 'best in the world'.

items.p: Two spinners both have an average fall time of 1.5 seconds. Spinner A's times range from 1.4 to 1.6. Spinner B's times range from 1.0 to 2.0. What is the best thing to say?
opts: Spinner A's times are steadier, because their range is smaller
They are exactly the same spinner
items.why: The averages match, but the range shows that B wobbles much more. The range tells you how much to trust a single drop.

items.p: Children with bigger shoes score higher in a reading test. What is the best explanation?
opts: Age may lie behind both, because older children have bigger feet and read better
items.why: Two things that go together do not have to cause each other. A third thing, age, can sit behind both.

items.p: A bean plant in the sun grew an average of 5 centimetres in a week, in 3 pots. A bean plant in the shade grew 2 centimetres in 3 pots. Each set ranged by about 1 centimetre. Write a claim, evidence and a limit.
items.a: Claim: in our test, bean plants in the sun grew taller than those in the shade. Evidence: the averages were 5 and 2 centimetres, a gap of 3, bigger than the spread of about 1. Limit: we tested one kind of bean for one week.
items.why: A strong answer has a claim that answers the question, evidence with numbers, and a limit that says what was not tested.

items.p: One bridge held 10, 12, 11, 11 and 31 coins in five tries. What should you do first?
opts: Check what happened in the 31 coin try and repeat it
Report the average of 15 without comment
items.why: The 31 is far from the others. It may be a slip or a real result. Check and repeat before deciding. Reporting only the average of 15 would hide the odd one.

items.p: Judge each conclusion.
items.why: A conclusion is supported when the gap between results is bigger than the wobble, and it stays within what was tested. It goes too far when it claims more. It cannot be told when the evidence is too small or too wobbly.
items: One try each: warm water dissolved sugar faster than cold, so warm water is always faster.
Three bridges of shape A held 11, 12 and 13 coins and three of shape B held 4, 5 and 4, so A held more in our test.
A coin gave 6 heads in 10 tosses, so it is unfair.
All the plants in the sun grew taller than the plants in the dark, in a test of 20 plants each.
Two plates of identical seeds sprouted 7 and 9, so the second plate had better seeds.
Spinners with long wings fell slower, so all objects with long wings fall slower.

items.p: A test is ____ if you get about the same results each time you repeat it.
items.why: Reliable results are steady. A test that gives different results each time cannot be trusted, even if it is fair.

items.p: Two settings are enough to see the shape of a pattern.
items.why: False. Two points can always be joined by a straight line, however the real pattern behaves. A third point can show a bend or a flat part.

items.p: A girl tests different amounts of salt in water to see how long a potato slice takes to rise. Which kind of graph shows the shape best?
items.why: The amount of salt can sit anywhere along a line, so a line graph shows how the time changes. A bar chart is best for separate things such as different shapes.

items.p: Put these steps for finding an average in order.
a: Add them up to get the total
Count how many numbers there are
Divide the total by how many there are
items.why: You need the numbers first. Then you add them, count them, and divide. The count is easy to forget.
items: Count how many numbers there are
Divide the total by how many there are
Add them up to get the total

items.p: A spinner with 4 centimetre wings took an average of 12 tenths of a second, one with 6 centimetre wings took 16, and one with 8 centimetre wings took 21. Draw a line graph of these averages, with labelled axes.
items.a: A graph with wing length (cm) along the bottom and average time (tenths of a second) up the side, with dots at (4, 12), (6, 16), (8, 21) joined by straight lines.
items.why: A strong graph labels both axes with units, gives a title, plots the averages and joins the dots. It rises steadily.
items.art: A line graph with three dots joined by straight lines rising from left to right.

items.p: Match each source of wobble to an example.
items.why: Every real measurement has several sources of wobble. A good test keeps the big ones small and repeats the test to deal with the rest.
pairs: Small change in the starting hand
the spinner leaves the hand a little tilted
Slip in measuring
the stopwatch is pressed a fraction late
Moving air
a draught carries the spinner sideways
Differences in the paper
one strip is a little thicker than another

items.p: Three of these help protect a test from hopeful measuring. Which is the odd one out?
opts: Write the prediction before the test
Use a helper who does not know which spinner is which
Tell the timer which spinner should win
Share the numbers for others to check
items.why: Telling the timer what to expect invites the timer's hope to bend the result. The other three guard against it.

items.p: Why do scientists use a blind test?
opts: So the person measuring cannot let hope push the result
items.why: If the measurer does not know which thing is which, they cannot lean towards the one they hope will win.

items.p: A girl finds that the tulsi pot corner had about one fewer mosquito a night, while the nightly counts ranged from 2 to 9. One friend says 'tulsi works'. Another says 'we cannot tell'. Who do you agree with?
items.a: A strong answer notes that the gap is smaller than the wobble, so the claim goes beyond the evidence, and suggests more nights or a bigger change. Kavya's hope is natural, but it should not bend the conclusion.
items.why: Pick-a-side questions have no single right side. Marks go for comparing the gap with the wobble and for stating the other view fairly.

views.says: Fewer mosquitoes in the tulsi corner is what we expected. The numbers agree, so tulsi probably works.
The nightly counts swing by much more than the difference of one. We cannot tell chance from a real effect, so we should keep counting.

items.ask: Which friend is closer to what the numbers show, and what would you do next?

items.p: Explain in your own words why hoping for an answer can bend a test, and describe one way to guard against it.
items.a: When we hope for an answer, small choices like when we press the stopwatch can lean towards it without us noticing. We can use a blind test, in which a helper does not know which thing is which.
items.why: A strong answer says the bending is unintended and gives a concrete guard, such as a blind test, writing predictions first, or sharing the numbers.

items.p: An odd result that appears again when you repeat the test is probably real.
items.why: True. A fluke is unlikely to happen twice. If an odd result repeats, it may be the most interesting finding of the test.

items.p: Which conclusion states its limit?
opts: In our test of three wing lengths, the longest wings gave the slowest fall
The longest wing always gives the slowest fall
items.why: The first conclusion says what was tested. 'Always' claims more than three wing lengths can show.

items.p: Two designs have averages of 20 and 25 and each set spreads by about 8. What is the best thing to say?
opts: The gap of 5 is smaller than the spread, so we cannot tell yet
The second design is clearly bigger
The first design is clearly bigger
items.why: When the gap between averages is smaller than the spread, chance could explain it. More tries or a bigger change are needed.

items.p: Plan the three jobs for this question: does the size of a paper boat change how many coins it holds before it sinks?
items.a: Change: the size of the boat. Measure: the number of coins held. Keep the same: the paper type, the shape, the basin of water, and the way coins are added. Repeat each size three times.
items.why: A strong answer names one thing to change, one thing to measure with a unit, and a list of things kept the same.

items.p: Is this a hidden difference that spoils a fair test of which cloth dries faster?
items.why: The test changes the kind of cloth, so the cotton and the nylon is the point of the test. A difference in wetness or place would also change the drying time.
items: One cloth hangs near a fan and the other in a corner
Both cloths are the same size
One cloth is wetter than the other
Both cloths hang side by side in the same room
One is made of cotton and the other of nylon

items.p: A company gets a test result that its new product is not much better than the old one. A manager wants to leave that result out of the report. A scientist wants to report it. Who do you agree with?
items.a: A strong answer says that hiding results gives a false picture, and may harm people who rely on the product. The manager's worry about confusion can be met by explaining the result clearly.
items.why: Pick-a-side questions have no single right side. Marks go for thinking about who is affected and for stating the other view fairly.

views.says: The report should show good news. The odd result will confuse the customers.
A result that does not fit is still a result. Leaving it out would give people a false picture.

items.ask: What could happen if odd results are left out of reports?

items.p: Five bridge tries held 12, 12, 13, 12 and 25 coins. What is the average with all five, and without the 25?
opts: 15 with all five, and 12.25 without the 25
items.why: With all five, 74 divided by 5 is 14.8, about 15. Without the 25, 49 divided by 4 is about 12.25. The odd 25 pulls the average up, so check it before reporting.

items.p: Repeating a test many times removes all the wobble from the results.
items.why: False. Repeating does not remove the wobble. It lets the highs and lows balance in the average, so the average is steadier than any single try.

items.p: The biggest number minus the smallest number in a set is called the ____.
items.why: The range shows how far the numbers spread. A big range means a big wobble.

items.p: Three of these are good habits for writing a conclusion. Which one is the odd one out?
opts: Use words such as 'in our test'
Say what you did not test
Claim it is true for everything
items.why: A conclusion should say no more than the results show. Claiming something is true for everything goes far beyond a single test.

items.p: Put these in a good order for dealing with an odd result.
a: Look for a reason, such as a bump
Decide whether to keep it or explain it
items.why: Write it down first, so it cannot disappear. Then look for a reason, then repeat, and only then decide.
items: Decide whether to keep it or explain it
Look for a reason, such as a bump

items.p: Match each situation to the kind of thing it is.
items.why: A pattern, chance, a cause and bias are four different things. A fair test, repeating and blind measuring help to tell them apart.
pairs: Children with bigger shoes read better
a pattern, with age behind both
A coin gives 7 heads in 10 tosses
chance
Longer wings, slower fall, in a fair test
a cause that we can test
One helper hopes for a result
a source of bias

items.p: A girl tests 0, 1 and 3 teaspoons of water on seeds. The sprouted counts are 0, 8 and 8 out of 10. What does this suggest?
opts: Some water helps, but more than one teaspoon may make no difference
items.why: The jump from 0 to 8 is big. The step from 1 to 3 teaspoons is zero. Trying three settings revealed that the gain levels off.

items.p: Describe a time in a test when repeating a measurement would have changed your conclusion.
items.a: For example: if we only dropped the spinner once and it took 2.4 seconds, we might think it was slow. After five drops with times from 1.4 to 2.4, we see that 2.4 was the high end of the wobble.
items.why: A strong answer shows that a single try can mislead, and that the repeats show where the typical value lies.

items.p: Four bridge shapes held on average 1, 8, 15 and 17 coins. Draw a bar chart with the shapes flat, channel, pleated and tube, and label the axes.
items.a: A bar chart with four bars of heights 1, 8, 15 and 17, labelled flat, channel, pleated and tube, with the vertical axis labelled coins held.
items.why: A bar chart suits separate shapes. A strong chart labels both axes and gives a title, with the bars drawn to scale.
items.art: A bar chart with four bars rising from left to right labelled with bridge shapes.

items.p: In one class, taller children also had bigger shoe sizes. What is the best thing to say?

open_questions.q: Is the wobble in a measurement only our ignorance of tiny details, or is some of it built into nature?
open_questions.why_open: In everyday life, the wobble comes from small causes we cannot track. In quantum physics, some outcomes seem to be random in a deeper way. Physicists still argue about what that means.

open_questions.q: How many repeats are enough, in a world where every test is different?
open_questions.why_open: Statisticians have rules for many kinds of test. But no rule fits every case, and scientists still debate how strict they should be.

open_questions.q: How many published results are wrong, because of chance, because of hopeful measuring, or because odd results were left out?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists who study how well results can be repeated have found that some do not hold up. Nobody knows exactly how often, and the answer differs between fields.

open_questions.q: Which other old remedies hold a real clue, and how can they be tested fairly?
open_questions.why_open: Tu Youyou's story shows that an old text can hold a real clue, but most old remedies do not work. Sorting the good clues from the rest takes careful, fair tests, and much of that work is still to be done.

open_questions.q: Can a test be fair if the thing you want to change cannot be changed, such as the weather or a person's age?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists compare many cases or wait for nature to make the change. People still argue about how strong such evidence can be.

open_questions.q: Why do people trust a single story more than a long run of numbers?
open_questions.why_open: Psychologists have studied this for decades. Stories feel real, and numbers feel abstract, but nobody has a complete answer or a sure cure.

maths.problem: Five drops of a spinner took 14, 16, 15, 13 and 17 tenths of a second. What is the average time, and what is the range?
maths.answer: The average is 15 tenths, which is 1.5 seconds. The range is 4 tenths.
maths.explain: 14 plus 16 plus 15 plus 13 plus 17 is 75. 75 divided by 5 is 15. The biggest is 17 and the smallest is 13, and 17 take away 13 is 4.
maths.context: In the Paper Spinner test, you drop each spinner five times and work out the average and the range.
maths.why_maths: The average gives one steady number for five different tries, and the range tells you how much to trust it.

maths.problem: Spinner A took an average of 14 tenths, with times from 12 to 16. Spinner B took an average of 19 tenths, with times from 17 to 21. Is the gap between the averages bigger than the spread within each set?
maths.answer: Yes. The gap is 5. The spread within each set is 4. So B is probably really slower.
maths.explain: 19 take away 14 is 5. In A, 16 take away 12 is 4. In B, 21 take away 17 is 4. The gap of 5 is bigger than the spread of 4, which suggests the difference is more than wobble. A gap of 5 against a spread of 4 is only just bigger, so more drops would help.
maths.context: After the Paper Spinner test, you compare two spinners and ask whether the difference is real.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the gap with the spread is how you decide whether a difference is real or could be chance.

maths.problem: Five bridge tries held 10, 12, 11, 11 and 31 coins. Find the average of all five. Then find the average without the 31. Which would you report, and what would you say?
maths.answer: All five: 15 coins. Without the 31: 11 coins. Report both, and say that the 31 was odd and needed checking.
maths.explain: 10 plus 12 plus 11 plus 11 plus 31 is 75, and 75 divided by 5 is 15. Without the 31, the sum is 44, and 44 divided by 4 is 11. The 31 pulls the average up by 4. You should check it, repeat it, and say what you did.
maths.context: In the Paper Bridge test, you may see one try that is far from the others.
maths.why_maths: Working out the average with and without the odd result shows how much one number can pull an average, so you know why to check it.

maths.problem: Over 14 evenings, a tulsi corner had 71 mosquitoes in total and the other corner had 84. About how many more per night was that? The nightly counts ran from 2 to 9, so the range was 7. Is the difference per night bigger or smaller than the range?
maths.answer: About 1 more per night. It is much smaller than the range of 7. So the difference is much smaller than the nightly wobble.
maths.explain: 84 take away 71 is 13. 13 divided by 14 is a little less than 1. The nightly counts spread by 7, so a difference of about 1 is far smaller than the swings.
maths.context: In a story, a girl counted mosquitoes in two balcony corners for fourteen evenings and found a small difference.
maths.why_maths: Dividing the total difference by the number of nights shows how big the difference is per night, so it can be compared with the wobble.

maths.problem: Two plates of ten identical seeds with the same water gave 7 and 9 sprouted seeds. What share of each plate sprouted? How many percentage points apart are the two plates?
maths.answer: 70 out of 100 and 90 out of 100. They are 20 percentage points apart, and they had identical treatment.
maths.explain: 7 out of 10 is 70 out of 100, and 9 out of 10 is 90 out of 100. 90 take away 70 is 20. Two plates treated the same already differ by 20 percentage points, so a gap of 20 between two different treatments proves little.
maths.context: In the Thirsty Seeds project and the Coin Wobble activity, you see that identical treatments can give different counts.
maths.why_maths: Turning counts into shares makes plates of different sizes comparable, and shows how big the chance wobble can be.

maths.problem: The averages for spinners with wings of 4, 6 and 8 centimetres were 12, 16 and 21 tenths of a second. Estimate the average for a 5 centimetre wing. Why is this a safer guess than one for a 20 centimetre wing?
maths.answer: About 14 tenths. It is between two tested points, but 20 centimetres is far outside anything tested.
maths.explain: A 5 centimetre wing sits halfway between 4 and 6. Halfway between 12 and 16 is 14. For 20 centimetres, the pattern might bend or level off, and we have no evidence out there.
maths.context: In the Paper Spinner test, you draw a line graph of wing length against average fall time.
maths.why_maths: Reading a value between tested points shows what a line graph is for, and why guesses beyond the data are risky.

maths.problem: A paper bridge with 0 pleats held 2 coins. With 2 pleats it held 10 coins. With 4 pleats it held 18 coins. If the pattern continued, how many would 6 pleats hold? Would you trust that guess?
maths.answer: 26 coins. But I would not trust it without testing, because the pattern may not continue.
maths.explain: The numbers go up by 8 each time we add 2 pleats. 18 plus 8 is 26. But a strip only has so much width, and more pleats may make the folds too narrow to help. Only a test can show.
maths.context: In the Paper Bridge test, you may find that more pleats hold more coins in a steady pattern.
maths.why_maths: Continuing a number pattern gives a prediction to test, and reminds you that patterns can stop.

maths.problem: A test has 3 settings with 5 drops each. Each drop and reset takes about 20 seconds. About how many minutes will all the drops take?
maths.explain: 3 times 5 is 15 drops. 15 times 20 seconds is 300 seconds. 300 seconds divided by 60 is 5 minutes.
maths.context: Before the Paper Spinner test, you plan how long the drops will take.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying the number of tries by the time for each shows how long a repeated test will take, so you can plan your session.

maths.problem: In five sets of ten coin tosses, the heads were 4, 6, 7, 3 and 5. What is the average number of heads, and what is the range?
maths.answer: The average is 5 heads. The range is 4.
maths.explain: 4 plus 6 plus 7 plus 3 plus 5 is 25. 25 divided by 5 is 5. The biggest is 7 and the smallest is 3, and 7 take away 3 is 4.
maths.context: In the Coin Wobble activity, you toss a coin in sets of ten and see how the counts spread.
maths.why_maths: Seeing that the average is 5 while single sets range by 4 shows how much a single set can mislead.

maths.problem: Your stopwatch time could be wrong by up to 2 tenths of a second on each drop. Two spinners have times of 15 and 18 tenths. Could the real gap be zero?
maths.answer: Yes, it could. The gap of 3 could be reduced by up to 4 tenths, if one time was 2 too low and the other 2 too high.
maths.explain: The first time could really be 17 and the second 16, which are close. The gap of 3 is smaller than the possible combined error of 4. Averaging several drops reduces the effect.
maths.context: In the Paper Spinner test, the person with the stopwatch reacts a little late or early on every drop.
maths.why_maths: Adding up the possible errors on both times shows when a gap is too small to trust, and why we average several tries.

how_we_found_out.story: In 1969, Tu Youyou, a Chinese pharmacologist, joined a secret national project to find a medicine for malaria. Her team tested hundreds of plant extracts on infected mice. Sweet wormwood, an old Chinese herb, looked promising at first, but the results were uneven. People usually prepared herbal medicines by boiling or heating. Tu went back to an old handbook written by Ge Hong more than 1,600 years ago. It said to soak the herb in cold water and wring out the juice. She guessed that heat might be destroying the part that works. So she changed one thing, the heat of the extraction, and kept the plant the same. In 1971 a low-heat extract worked very well on infected animals. Tu and colleagues reportedly tried it on themselves first, to check it was safe. The medicine, artemisinin, now treats malaria around the world. Tu shared the Nobel Prize in 2015.
how_we_found_out.who: Tu Youyou, a Chinese pharmacologist, and her research team
how_we_found_out.when: 1969 to 1971, and the Nobel Prize in 2015
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Herbal medicines were usually prepared by heating or boiling, so heated extracts of sweet wormwood gave uneven results and some people thought the herb was not useful. Tu's team found that the heat was spoiling the active part, and a gentler extraction worked.

roots.context: We have dropped spinners again and again, found averages and ranges, and learned to say no more than the numbers say. Now we ask what the wobble in every measurement tells us about the world and about ourselves.

deep_truth.truth: Drop the same spinner from the same hand five times and you get five different times. Nothing was changed, and still nothing repeated exactly. A measurement is not one exact number. It is a small spread of numbers, and the honest answer is the whole spread.
deep_truth.habit: We think a measured number is the true size of the thing, like a label stuck on it. But the number changes each time we measure, so what we really have is a spread.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Paper Spinner test, the same spinner gave different times on every drop. The coin tosses gave different counts of heads in every set of ten. Only the average and the range described what was steady and what wobbled.

three.who_am_i: Count your breaths for one minute, three times, and you will get three different numbers. You are not one number. You are a spread, and so is everything about you.
three.what_is_life: No two leaves, seeds or children are exactly alike. Living beings vary from one to the next, and that variety lets a kind of living being survive when the world changes.
three.what_is_this_world: Air moves, hands shake and tiny causes pile up. Exact sameness is rare in the world, so careful people measure many times.

roots.thread: Think of the five falls of the spinner. Each fall was the paper, the air in the room, your hand and your eye meeting for a moment. No two meetings were quite the same, because the room, the hand and the eye are always moving a little. One number from one meeting hides that. Many numbers show it. The world is not a row of identical copies. It is a crowd of things that are similar and never the same. The pattern we find is not one point. It is the shape of the crowd.

teachings.teaching: A group of blind men each touched a different part of an elephant. Each described the elephant as something different, such as a pillar, a rope or a fan. Each was sure he knew the elephant, and they began to quarrel.
teachings.link: Each drop of the spinner is like one touch. It gives a true part of the picture, and no more. Many drops together give the shape of the whole.

teachings.teaching: The Gita teaches evenness of mind in success and in failure, and calls this evenness yoga.
teachings.link: A scientist who hopes for one answer can lean towards it. Staying even about whether the result is the hoped-for one helps the test stay honest.

teachings.teaching: Confucius told his student that knowing means this: when you know something, to hold that you know it, and when you do not know something, to allow that you do not know it.
teachings.link: A conclusion that says only what the results show follows this teaching. 'We cannot tell yet' is also knowledge.

science.text: Every real measurement has some uncertainty. Scientists report a result together with its spread, and not as a single exact number.
In quantum physics, some outcomes seem to be random in a deeper way than ordinary wobble, but what that means is still debated.

other_view.who: Pierre-Simon Laplace, a French mathematician, in 1814
other_view.view: Laplace imagined a mind that knew every cause in the world at one moment. For such a mind, nothing would be uncertain, and the future would be as clear as the past. On this view the wobble is only our ignorance of small causes. It is not part of how the world is.

playtest: Read and walked through as a parent and child in a city flat would use it, but not yet tried at home by a family. Paper Spinner: strips of 4 by 16 centimetres cut with a slit of 4, 6 or 8 centimetres make three spinners with the same paper and clip weight. They spin when dropped from a grown-up's reach, and longer wings give slower falls, usually by a few tenths of a second. Times of about 1 to 2.5 seconds are normal. Stopwatch reaction adds a wobble of about 0.2 seconds, which is the point of the repeats. If a spinner tumbles, bend its wings further apart. Close the windows and switch off the fan. Paper Bridge: 9.5 by 21 centimetre strips over a 15 centimetre gap. The flat strip holds very little. The channel, the pleated fan and the tube hold many more, though which is best may differ. A fresh strip is used each try. Thirsty Seeds: moong seeds sprout in 2 to 4 days in warm weather. Dry seeds should not sprout. A little and plenty may give similar counts, which is an honest result. Wash hands, and do not eat mouldy seeds. The Sneaky Variable and the table activities need no waiting. Coin Wobble counts usually run between 3 and 7 heads. The Mosquitoes and the Tulsi is made up, and so are its counts. Facts to verify: the Tu Youyou dates (1969 joined, 1971 low-heat extract worked, 2015 Nobel Prize), the age of Ge Hong's handbook (about 340 CE), the reported self-test, the Laplace date (1814), and the Udana, Gita and Analects references. Videos are marked find-id because no id was known for certain.
